concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Distinguish a graft from a flap by blood supply
concepts.learningObjective: Classify supplied reconstructive tissue transfers by whether blood supply is retained or carried and reconnected, rather than by donor identity or location.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Explain epithelial regrowth at a split-thickness donor site
concepts.learningObjective: Explain how retained donor-site skin appendage epithelium contributes to resurfacing after a split-thickness harvest, separately from recipient-graft vascularization.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Explain an IgE-mediated type I reaction
concepts.learningObjective: Connect a documented IgE-mediated type I reaction to mast-cell activation rather than infer the mechanism from a rash alone.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.learningObjective: Recognize specialist-confirmed allergic contact dermatitis as T-cell-mediated type IV hypersensitivity and distinguish it from an IgE reaction.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.learningObjective: Recognize a hand laceration with an abnormal active-tendon examination as outside routine clinic closure.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.learningObjective: Evaluate wound depth, contamination, foreign material risk, and distal structural function before routine closure.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Coverage when the recipient bed cannot support a graft
concepts.learningObjective: Choose a reconstructive approach that transfers perfused tissue when the recipient bed cannot support avascular skin transfer.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Perfusion after a completely detached tissue transfer
concepts.learningObjective: Identify the vascular reconnection needed by a completely detached vessel-bearing flap rather than apply graft or pedicled-flap assumptions.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: A collagen cofactor is not universal postoperative therapy
concepts.learningObjective: Distinguish an established nutrient requirement from evidence that every adequately nourished postoperative patient needs high-dose supplementation.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Recipient-vessel selection for a free transfer
concepts.learningObjective: Use separate arterial and venous continuity findings to select a functional recipient pair for a proposed free transfer.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.learningObjective: Infer an outflow concern from several interval observations rather than assume a sound arterial signal certifies the circulation. Seek urgent operative assessment of a potentially correctable pedicle problem rather than substitute selected adjunctive decompression or surveillance.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: A recipient bed that changes before coverage
concepts.learningObjective: Distinguish the original avascular cortical surface from the currently prepared tissue-covered surface and assess the remaining structural requirements. Choose coverage based on the current recipient bed rather than automatically import a flap because the first debridement exposed bone.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.learningObjective: Recognize that wound care and tetanus vaccination-history assessment are separate required considerations.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Scored-objective override after reading the concept objective.

concepts.learningObjective: Explain the shift from relatively type III-rich early wound matrix toward type I collagen during remodeling in patient-specific scar counseling.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.learningObjective: Identify vitamin C as a cofactor for proline and lysine hydroxylation in collagen biosynthesis and connect inadequate hydroxylation with reduced collagen stability and impaired healing.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Distinguish raised scars by their boundary
concepts.learningObjective: Use extension beyond versus confinement within the original wound to distinguish a keloid from a hypertrophic scar.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.learningObjective: Identify a clinician-selected open wound healing without immediate or planned delayed edge approximation as secondary-intention healing.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

question.patientPresentation: A patient with markedly limited dietary variety has impaired wound healing, prompting a review of collagen biochemistry.
question.stem: Which consequence most directly follows from inadequate vitamin C availability during collagen synthesis?

answerChoices.label: Impaired proline and lysine hydroxylation, producing less stable collagen
Selective loss of type III collagen with normal type I collagen
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The vitamin C-dependent hydroxylation mechanism is not limited to type III collagen.

answerChoices.label: Excessive gamma-carboxylation of coagulation proteins
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Gamma-carboxylation is a vitamin K-dependent pathway and is not increased by vitamin C inadequacy.

answerChoices.label: Reduced intestinal calcium absorption causing immediate scar mineralization
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This combines an unrelated vitamin D mechanism with a consequence not produced by vitamin C-dependent collagen hydroxylation.

question.explanation: Inadequate ascorbate impairs proline and lysine hydroxylation, compromising normal collagen maturation and stability and thereby contributing to impaired healing.

question.patientPresentation: A postoperative patient asks what ascorbate actually does during collagen formation.
question.stem: Which explanation is most accurate?

answerChoices.label: It supports the activity of prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases needed for collagen maturation and stability
It becomes a structural amino acid within collagen
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Vitamin C is a cofactor; it is not incorporated into collagen as a structural amino acid.

answerChoices.label: It converts type I collagen into type III collagen
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Collagen types are not produced by vitamin C converting one mature type into another.

answerChoices.label: It activates vitamin K-dependent clotting factors
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation, not vitamin C, supports activation of those clotting proteins.

question.explanation: Vitamin C supports the hydroxylase enzymes required for normal collagen maturation and stability; it is neither a collagen amino acid nor a collagen-type converter.

question.stem: Which proposed coverage addresses the perfusion problem described for {patientName}'s recipient bed?

answerChoices.label: Pedicled tissue-flap coverage
answerChoices.rationale: A pedicled flap retains a vascular connection and therefore addresses a different perfusion requirement from a graft dependent on the bed.

answerChoices.label: Split-thickness skin-graft coverage
answerChoices.rationale: A graft has no transferred connected blood supply; changing thickness does not remove its dependence on recipient-bed support.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A graft has no transferred connected blood supply; changing thickness does not remove its dependence on recipient-bed support.

answerChoices.label: Full-thickness skin-graft coverage
answerChoices.rationale: This remains an avascular skin transfer dependent on the recipient bed rather than a tissue transfer retaining its vessels.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This remains an avascular skin transfer dependent on the recipient bed rather than a tissue transfer retaining its vessels.

question.explanation: A graft depends on the recipient bed for support and subsequent vascularization. A pedicled flap retains a vascular supply. Those facts explain the represented coverage choice; they do not provide a universal reconstructive algorithm or establish a particular flap's technical suitability.

question.stem: Which coverage plan fits {patientName}'s recorded wound surface and vessel map?
question.explanation: Evaluate the whole coverage surface and then the proposed tissue's circulation. The bleeding rim does not make the exposed central cortex equivalent to that rim. A graft depends on support from its bed; a pedicled flap transfers a connected supply. Both marked flaps reach, but design 1's route is divided and design 2's remains connected. design 2 therefore fits the supplied record. This is a constructed perfusion problem, not a claim that an unnamed flap is universally suitable for an anterior-shin defect; actual anatomy and coverage selection require specialist confirmation.

exhibit.description: Constructed anterior-shin wound map. The central exposed cortical surface and bleeding muscle rim are shown. Flap design 1 reaches the defect but its feeding vessel ends at a ligature. Flap design 2 also reaches the defect and its feeding vessel remains continuous with an artery outside the injury zone.
exhibit.caption: Original constructed operative sketch; not a patient photograph or an anatomic flap atlas

answerChoices.label: Local fasciocutaneous flap on design 2
answerChoices.rationale: This plan transfers vascularized tissue with an uninterrupted feeding route into the wound; both reach and the vessel connection are represented.

answerChoices.label: Local fasciocutaneous flap on design 1
answerChoices.rationale: Its tissue can reach, but the mapped feeding route is interrupted. Reach is not evidence of retained perfusion.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Its tissue can reach, but the mapped feeding route is interrupted. Reach is not evidence of retained perfusion.

answerChoices.label: Split-thickness skin graft across the central defect
answerChoices.rationale: The vascular muscle rim does not establish vascular support across the exposed central cortical surface. The graft does not bring its own connected supply.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The vascular muscle rim does not establish vascular support across the exposed central cortical surface. The graft does not bring its own connected supply.

question.stem: Which coverage procedure best fits {patientName}'s current recipient findings?
question.explanation: Read the recipient bed at the time of definitive coverage, rather than carry the first debridement's state forward. Skin grafts depend on their recipient surface, and bare nonbleeding cortex differs from a continuous prepared vascular layer over that cortex. The current shallow represented surface supports a split-thickness graft among these choices. Both flap alternatives are viable, so vessel connectivity does not select the key. The exact current-bed graft suitability is a targeted reconstructive source/clinician hold; this is not an operative plan from a schematic.

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations
cells: Bare cortical bone without punctate bleeding; surrounding muscle bled
A continuous adherent layer of red tissue covers the former cortical surface and bleeds in fine points on gentle preparation
Shallow surface defect away from a moving joint; tendon and fixation material are covered; no space needing bulk replacement
A local muscle transfer and a free anterolateral-thigh transfer have usable mapped supplies; neither pedicle has been ligated

answerChoices.label: Coverage using a split-thickness skin graft
answerChoices.rationale: The current prepared surface differs from the originally bare cortex and can support graft coverage without importing unnecessary tissue bulk.

answerChoices.label: Coverage using a pedicled local muscle flap
answerChoices.rationale: This could cover a poorly supporting bed or fill a space, but the old bare-bone finding is no longer the whole current recipient assessment.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This could cover a poorly supporting bed or fill a space, but the old bare-bone finding is no longer the whole current recipient assessment.

answerChoices.label: Coverage using a free anterolateral-thigh flap
answerChoices.rationale: A viable free-transfer plan is not selected simply because the original bed once lacked support; the current superficial defect can be treated less extensively.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A viable free-transfer plan is not selected simply because the original bed once lacked support; the current superficial defect can be treated less extensively.

question.stem: Which recipient pair should be used for {patientName}'s flap artery and vein in this mapped plan?
question.explanation: A free transfer needs a complete perfusion circuit, not just two technically reachable vessel ends. Trace continuity in each direction: A1 remains connected to arterial inflow, while V2 remains connected to venous return. The correct pair crosses the drawing's sides. Neither donor identity nor proximity of the ends establishes that circuit. Actual recipient selection also requires specialist assessment of vessel quality; this constructed drawing supplies caliber and reach, not a universal operative recipe.

exhibit.description: Constructed recipient-vessel map. An artery runs from the left source through A1 to a ligature, with A2 on the opposite disconnected segment. A vein has V1 left of its ligature; V2 on the right remains continuous with venous return. Arterial inflow is from the left and venous return is toward the right.
exhibit.caption: Original constructed vessel-continuity sketch; recipient ends are fictional

answerChoices.label: Flap artery to A1; flap vein to V2
answerChoices.rationale: This pair connects the flap to both arterial inflow and a continuous venous return route.

answerChoices.rationale: Arterial inflow is represented, but V1 ends at the venous ligature rather than a return route.

answerChoices.rationale: Venous return is represented, but the arterial ligature separates A2 from inflow.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Venous return is represented, but the arterial ligature separates A2 from inflow.

decisionNodes.explanation: A free transfer needs a complete perfusion circuit, not just two technically reachable vessel ends. Trace continuity in each direction: A1 remains connected to arterial inflow, while V2 remains connected to venous return. The correct pair crosses the drawing's sides. Neither donor identity nor proximity of the ends establishes that circuit. Actual recipient selection also requires specialist assessment of vessel quality; this constructed drawing supplies caliber and reach, not a universal operative recipe.

question.stem: Which next salvage strategy best fits {patientName}'s later flap findings?
question.explanation: Integrate the surface, blood and signal changes. Persisting arterial inflow does not establish that blood can leave the flap. The newly swollen purple tissue, rapid refill, dark bleeding and changed venous signal require urgent microsurgical assessment, with operative pedicle exploration the best offered next salvage strategy. This does not diagnose the exact thrombus, prescribe an anastomotic revision or establish a salvage-time threshold. The new interpretation and rescue ranking require targeted reconstructive-source verification.

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations
cells: Pink and soft; color returns after brief pressure
Small bright-red drop
Arterial and venous signals recorded
More swollen and purple; color returns almost immediately after pressure
Brisk dark blood
Arterial signal persists; previously recorded venous signal cannot be reproduced

answerChoices.label: Urgent operative pedicle exploration
answerChoices.rationale: The combined interval findings suggest impaired outflow despite persisting inflow; a potentially correctable early pedicle problem requires urgent microsurgical assessment and exploration.

answerChoices.label: Bedside medicinal-leech decompression
answerChoices.rationale: This may be used in selected outflow problems that cannot be surgically corrected, but does not first address the represented potentially correctable pedicle issue.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This may be used in selected outflow problems that cannot be surgically corrected, but does not first address the represented potentially correctable pedicle issue.

answerChoices.label: Serial surface-Doppler observation
answerChoices.rationale: A persisting arterial sound does not settle venous drainage; observation would delay assessment of a potentially salvageable vascular problem.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A persisting arterial sound does not settle venous drainage; observation would delay assessment of a potentially salvageable vascular problem.

question.stem: Which vitamin C recommendation is supported for {patientName}'s documented nutritional situation?

answerChoices.label: Maintain adequate intake after nutrition assessment
answerChoices.rationale: A biochemical requirement does not establish a therapeutic indication for universal high-dose supplementation in a well-nourished patient.

answerChoices.label: Add a high-dose course for the postoperative incision
answerChoices.rationale: This extends a cofactor requirement into an unsupported universal treatment rule.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This extends a cofactor requirement into an unsupported universal treatment rule.

answerChoices.label: Replace the nutrition assessment with a high-dose course
answerChoices.rationale: Supplementation is not a substitute for assessing actual nutritional risk or deficiency.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Supplementation is not a substitute for assessing actual nutritional risk or deficiency.

question.explanation: Ascorbate supports collagen hydroxylation, and deficiency can impair healing. Those facts do not demonstrate that all well-nourished postoperative patients benefit from routine high-dose treatment. No supplementation dose or deficiency-treatment regimen is authored here.

case.displayName: A collagen cofactor is not universal postoperative therapy
case.presentation: {patientName}, a 61-year-old woman, has an uncomplicated healing incision and a varied diet. Her perioperative nutritional assessment found no deficiency. She was advised to buy a high-dose vitamin C product because collagen synthesis requires ascorbate, and asks whether that fact establishes a need for the product.

decisionNodes.stem: A hand laceration has controlled bleeding, but the patient cannot actively flex the affected digit. What is the safest next step?

answerChoices.label: Do not treat it as a simple closure; arrange prompt higher-level tendon evaluation
Close the skin routinely and defer the motion deficit to a distant follow-up
Close the skin and defer the abnormal active-motion finding to a routine later visit
Prescribe antibiotics as treatment for the motion deficit

decisionNodes.explanation: An active-motion deficit makes this a possible tendon injury, not the simple laceration phenotype. Prompt higher-level evaluation is required before routine closure.

decisionNodes.stem: Before deciding whether to close this clean superficial hand wound, what should be done first?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: First operation
items.value: The anterior leg wound exposed a nonbleeding cortical surface after periosteal loss.

items.label: Interval course
items.value: A dermal regeneration template was placed after wound-bed preparation.

items.label: Current examination
items.value: The temporary silicone layer has been removed. A continuous adherent red tissue layer covers the former exposed cortex and bleeds throughout on gentle abrasion. The shallow wound lies away from a joint; surrounding skin cannot approximate without marked tension.

choices.label: Split-thickness skin-graft placement
choices.rationale: The current vascular covering changes the substrate from the original bare cortex; direct edge closure would create tension.
choices.temptation: Reassess the present bed and geometry rather than anchor on the first operation.
choices.counterfactual: A persistent uncovered cortical area would require additional preparation or vascularized tissue.

choices.label: Repeat dermal-template placement
choices.rationale: The record describes an incorporated vascular covering ready for its epithelial stage, not loss of the template over exposed cortex.
choices.temptation: Carry the old bare-bone problem forward after the bed has changed.
choices.counterfactual: Loss of the template with persistent nonvascular exposure would justify further bed preparation.

choices.label: Delayed primary suture closure
choices.rationale: Marked closure tension remains a competing mechanical problem even though the vascular layer now supports grafting.
choices.temptation: Equate vascular improvement with adequate tissue for direct closure.
choices.counterfactual: Freely mobile viable edges that approximate without excessive tension can support direct closure.

proposals.explanation: The first operation is historical. The current continuous bleeding layer supports the next epithelial coverage stage, while edge tension makes direct approximation unsuitable. This does not imply that all denuded cortex reliably becomes graftable.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: Covered the key and chronology: all options are real next procedures. The task does not say graft-ready. The historical avascular finding favors the closest wrong plan unless current observations are interpreted.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three next coverage procedures at the same reconstruction visit.
reasoningSteps: Identify that the current recipient substrate differs from the initial avascular cortex.
Combine the new bed with residual edge tension to select graft coverage rather than another preparation stage or forced closure.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Repeating a completed preparation stage because the original wound exposed bone.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: A continuous bleeding covering after template incorporation together with marked tension on edge approximation.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: If the silicone removal revealed nonvascular uncovered cortex, repeat preparation or vascularized coverage would replace grafting.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Deleting the current layer row restores the original uncertainty. Deleting edge tension makes direct closure a defensible competitor. No irrelevant vessel-ligation reassurance remains.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Standalone; the mixed-bed case is not an earlier scored companion and its explanation is not visible.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate/hard PGY-2/3 author prediction: Repeating a completed preparation stage because the original wound exposed bone. No measured difficulty or independent PASS is claimed.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: Resolved using a continuous bleeding covering after template incorporation together with marked tension on edge approximation. The counterfactual was re-solved against every offered option.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed the old all-purpose flap foils and explicit graft-eligibility conclusion. Re-solved the procedural alternatives with current observations; template-specific clinical suitability remains for Melissa.

proposals.reviewDisplay: key shown first for review only.

question.stem: Which coverage procedure best fits {patientName}'s current recipient findings?
question.explanation: Read the recipient bed at the time of definitive coverage, rather than carry the first debridement's state forward. Skin grafts depend on their recipient surface, and bare nonbleeding cortex differs from a continuous prepared vascular layer over that cortex. The current shallow represented surface supports a split-thickness graft among these choices. Both flap alternatives are viable, so vessel connectivity does not select the key. The exact current-bed graft suitability is a targeted reconstructive source/clinician hold; this is not an operative plan from a schematic.

answerChoices.label: Coverage using a split-thickness skin graft
answerChoices.rationale: The current prepared surface differs from the originally bare cortex and can support graft coverage without importing unnecessary tissue bulk.

answerChoices.label: Coverage using a pedicled local muscle flap
answerChoices.rationale: This could cover a poorly supporting bed or fill a space, but the old bare-bone finding is no longer the whole current recipient assessment.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This could cover a poorly supporting bed or fill a space, but the old bare-bone finding is no longer the whole current recipient assessment.

answerChoices.label: Coverage using a free anterolateral-thigh flap
answerChoices.rationale: A viable free-transfer plan is not selected simply because the original bed once lacked support; the current superficial defect can be treated less extensively.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: The task contains neither collection nor salvage. Two choices evacuate fluid and two retain the existing sheet, so neither a fluid-word match nor the sole-preservation shortcut selects the key. The full fictional examination is visible. The extra negative about grey tissue was removed; actual positive tissue observations carry the viability assessment.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three immediate local graft interventions.
reasoningSteps: Identify a newly developed graft-bed barrier rather than a failure of the originally vascular recipient bed.
Use the current tissue examination to choose attempted local salvage rather than discarding the lifted segment.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Evacuating the collection correctly but replacing a lifted segment merely because it is detached.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: The new interface pocket coexists with pink tissue and punctate dermal bleeding in the lifted portion.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: If the lifted segment were grey and nonbleeding on assessment, the retain-versus-replace judgment would change; if there were no interface fluid, a dressing-only correction could be appropriate.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Deleting tissue findings leaves replacement unresolved; deleting the pocket leaves no reason to open the interface. Intact epithelium alone is no longer used as a viability guarantee.

items.label: Bed and sheet
items.value: The wound bed remains red and punctately bleeding. The sheet contacts it with the wrist at rest.

items.label: Dynamic examination
items.value: Wrist flexion elongates the staple openings and translates the sheet across the bed; the overlying dressing shifts at the same time.

items.label: Fluid localization
items.value: A small fluid layer is recorded between the outer dressing and the sheet. Direct inspection shows contact at the sheet-bed interface at rest.

choices.label: Refix the sheet and add joint immobilization
choices.rationale: The displacement is reproduced by joint movement and loss of fixation. The recorded superficial fluid is not an intervening graft-bed collection.
choices.temptation: Localize the fluid before interpreting the moving interface.
choices.counterfactual: A deep collection lifting a stable sheet at rest would favor drainage; a nonviable bed would require reassessment and debridement.

choices.label: Fenestrate the sheet and drain the deep interface
choices.rationale: The current record places the fluid above the sheet. Opening the deep interface does not correct the reproducible translational movement.
choices.temptation: Repeat the earlier successful drainage without localizing the current fluid.
choices.counterfactual: A collection between graft and bed with persistent separation at rest would make drainage appropriate.

choices.label: Debride the recipient bed and regraft the defect
choices.rationale: The current bed is described as vascular; the new failure is linked to motion rather than demonstrated bed necrosis.
choices.temptation: Attribute repeated separation to failed recipient preparation.
choices.counterfactual: A devitalized bed on reassessment would change the reconstruction plan.

proposals.explanation: The fluid is above the sheet, while the loss of contact is reproduced by wrist movement and failing fixation. Refixation and joint support address that mechanism. Neither repeating deep drainage nor replacing a graft on an otherwise vascular bed corrects the demonstrated motion.

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: After release
items.value: Passive extension is restored. A small skin defect crosses the flexion crease, with a uniformly bleeding subcutaneous surface.

items.label: Neighboring tissue
items.value: Direct approximation recreates the flexed position. Adjacent local skin was involved in the original injury.

items.label: Donor assessment
items.value: A groin skin segment can cover the defect; its donor edges approximate without excessive tension.

choices.label: An unmeshed full-thickness autologous skin graft
choices.rationale: The well-supported small functional defect makes retaining dermis useful to limit later contraction; donor closure is feasible.
choices.temptation: Integrate the functional crease with the recipient and donor findings.
choices.counterfactual: A large defect with limited donor closure or less reliable recipient support can shift toward split-thickness coverage.

choices.label: An unmeshed thin split-thickness autologous skin graft
choices.rationale: A thin graft sacrifices dermal support and is more prone to secondary contraction at this recently released crease.
choices.temptation: Choose the graft that demands less support while neglecting the functional cost.
choices.counterfactual: A broad well-prepared area with limited donor skin and less functional contraction risk can favor a thinner graft.

choices.label: A widely meshed thin split-thickness autologous skin graft
choices.rationale: Expansion is not needed for this small defect and does not address recurrent contraction across the flexion crease.
choices.temptation: Import a large-surface donor-conservation strategy into a small functional reconstruction.
choices.counterfactual: Extensive coverage with scarce donor skin can justify an expanded meshed graft.

proposals.explanation: The same graft is not best for every surface. This small vascular defect crosses a functional crease, and retaining more dermis helps resist later contraction. The donor record resolves a real limitation of a full-thickness graft.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: All three are concrete autologous grafts of comparable scope. No option says less contraction; that inference is required. The task does not name a desired graft property.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three autologous graft preparations for the same coverage procedure.
reasoningSteps: Identify that recurrent contraction would reverse the functional gain from release.
Balance this need against the demonstrated bed support and ability to close a full-thickness donor defect.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Favoring thin expanded coverage despite a small high-function site with a suitable donor.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Small vascular crease defect and a donor site that can close without tension.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: With a broad defect and insufficient closable donor skin, a split-thickness graft becomes a more credible choice.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: The crease makes contraction consequential. Bed vascularity and closable donor edges are necessary eligibility observations; deleting either weakens the full-thickness choice.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Standalone. No earlier scar-treatment answer supplies the graft selection.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate/hard PGY-2/3 author prediction: Favoring thin expanded coverage despite a small high-function site with a suitable donor. No measured difficulty or independent PASS is claimed.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: Resolved using small vascular crease defect and a donor site that can close without tension. The counterfactual was re-solved against every offered option.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Compared actual graft strategies rather than a graft against a visibly severed flap. No claim of absolute superiority across all hand wounds or an exact harvest thickness.

proposals.task: Which functional assessment best addresses the structural risk before choosing {patientName}'s closure pathway?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Mechanism
items.value: A ceramic edge cut the palmar surface of a finger while it was curled tightly around a handle.

items.label: Initial observation
items.value: The small skin opening is now examined with the finger straight. The resting finger cascade looks similar to the other hand.

items.label: Reported function
items.value: The patient can move the finger during light activities but feels focal pain when pulling a loaded handle.

choices.label: Test PIP and DIP flexion separately against resistance
choices.rationale: An injured flexor may still allow gross movement. Testing its separate joint functions against resistance addresses an occult partial injury; neurovascular and wound assessments remain necessary.
choices.temptation: Integrate the palmar mechanism with preserved low-load movement.
choices.counterfactual: A dorsal injury with an extension deficit would direct specific extensor testing instead.

choices.label: Test a composite finger grip against resistance
choices.rationale: A global grip does not isolate each tendon function. Preserved movement or contribution from other structures can obscure the suspected deficit.
choices.temptation: Choose a load test but allow composite movement to mask individual function.
choices.counterfactual: Composite grip may be useful in a broader examination after individual tendon functions are assessed.

choices.label: Test PIP and DIP extension separately against resistance
choices.rationale: This is a real tendon assessment, but it chiefly addresses the extensor apparatus rather than the structures threatened by this palmar injury and load symptom.
choices.temptation: Choose isolated testing but localize the risk to the wrong tendon compartment.
choices.counterfactual: A dorsal laceration with impaired extension would make extensor assessment the relevant target.

proposals.explanation: The palmar mechanism localizes concern to flexor structures. Light movement and an apparently normal resting cascade do not exclude partial injury. Assess PIP and DIP flexion independently against resistance, alongside the complete wound and neurovascular examination; the result does not prescribe a repair technique.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: All three concrete maneuvers are unperformed, so no completed-test checklist reveals the key. Two choices test flexion and two use isolated joint assessment; anatomical localization and isolation both matter.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three specific functional examination maneuvers.
reasoningSteps: Localize the potentially injured functional compartment from the palmar cut and loaded-flexion symptom.
Choose an isolated loaded assessment because preserved light or composite movement can mask partial tendon injury.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Choosing resisted composite grip: it tests load but does not isolate the individual functions at risk.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: A palmar finger injury produces pain under load despite light movement and a near-normal resting posture.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: A dorsal cut with impaired extension would favor isolated extensor assessment; complete painless isolated flexor testing and adequate wound exploration would support a different closure pathway.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Removing the palmar mechanism weakens compartment localization. Removing the discrepancy between light and loaded movement loses the reason not to accept composite function alone.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Standalone clinic chart review. All earlier scored companions are removed. This node supplies the history it needs; no preceding feedback is visible.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate author prediction: near error is a real resisted flexion assessment that lacks isolation. This is not claimed hard or independently passed.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: The stated observations distinguish the nearest competing action: A palmar finger injury produces pain under load despite light movement and a near-normal resting posture. Counterfactual re-solve: A dorsal cut with impaired extension would favor isolated extensor assessment; complete painless isolated flexor testing and adequate wound exploration would support a different closure pathway.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Named PIP and DIP flexion explicitly, replaced passive/composite tests already supplied as completed results, and retained complete examination context. No unverified percentage of tendon damage or repair cutoff is used. The same repair attempt includes a final label scan: parallel length/category and removal of avoidable key-only noun matching.

case.learningSummary: What it is: A traumatic laceration is a cut through skin or underlying tissue; this pilot's simple form excludes infection, uncontrolled bleeding, and established deeper injury. Typical presentation: The simple phenotype is a recent superficial cut in a stable adult with controlled bleeding and intact distal function. Initial evaluation: Assess mechanism, location, depth, contamination, foreign material concern, and distal tendon and nerve function; separately review wound category and tetanus history. Management in this clinic: Provide basic wound care and routine closure only when the wound is within capability; apply or arrange CDC-supported tetanus prophylaxis. Red flags requiring urgent care: Abnormal active motion, new distal numbness, uncontrolled bleeding, or suspected deeper injury requires higher-level evaluation. Gross contamination requires deliberate cleaning and risk assessment and may exceed clinic capability.

items.label: Examination
items.value: The small palmar cut is accompanied by painful weak isolated finger flexion against resistance; active flexion remains possible.

items.label: Inspection attempt
items.value: Local anesthesia allowed inspection of the skin opening, but the deep flexor surface could not be fully seen.

items.label: Imaging record
items.value: Radiographs showed no fracture. The ultrasound report described continuity in the visualized tendon, but the segment beneath the wound was obscured by air and was not assessed.

choices.label: Splint and refer directly for hand-surgery assessment
choices.rationale: The negative observations do not cover the clinically suspicious segment. Protect the hand and obtain specialist assessment rather than use incomplete imaging as a referral gate.
choices.temptation: Interpret what each negative test actually assessed.
choices.counterfactual: Adequate visualization of the injured segment plus a complete painless normal examination could support a superficial-wound pathway.

choices.label: Splint and obtain repeat ultrasound before hand referral
choices.rationale: Repeat imaging can be a useful adjunct, but referral should not depend on a negative screen when clinical concern and incomplete exploration persist.
choices.temptation: Recognize the limited scan but make imaging clearance the prerequisite for specialist assessment.
choices.counterfactual: An adequately assessed low-risk injury with no unresolved tendon concern may be investigated without that same referral presumption.

choices.label: Splint and obtain MRI before hand referral
choices.rationale: Changing imaging modality does not remove the existing need for specialist assessment of a possible flexor laceration. The question is disposition, not a prohibition on adjunctive imaging.
choices.temptation: Seek a definitive-looking test before acting on unresolved clinical risk.
choices.counterfactual: MRI may be selected by the treating specialist when additional anatomical information will change management.

proposals.explanation: A report of continuity applies to the segment actually seen. Here the wound-level segment remains unassessed, the inspection was limited, and resisted function is abnormal. Splinting and prompt hand assessment remain appropriate. Ultrasound or MRI may add information; neither should be used to withhold referral until a lesion is demonstrated.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: Every option protects the hand and starts a prompt assessment pathway. Routine delay and mobilization caricatures are removed. The report identifies the actual unassessed anatomy rather than asserting that all imaging is unreliable.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three protected hand-injury disposition pathways.
reasoningSteps: Recognize that the negative radiograph and partial ultrasound do not assess the clinically suspicious tendon segment.
Keep protection and specialist assessment in the disposition plan instead of making a repeat image the prerequisite for referral.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Ordering prompt repeat ultrasound but using its result as a condition for hand referral.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Painful weak resisted flexion persists, and neither limited wound inspection nor the ultrasound visualized the wound-level tendon.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: A completely visualized superficial injury with normal painless isolated function could support routine wound care; an adequate specialist study can also guide treatment without being a prerequisite for initial assessment.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Removing the limited segment changes how much reassurance the ultrasound provides. Removing abnormal loaded function reduces the reason to sustain concern despite gross movement.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Standalone clinic chart review. All earlier scored companions are removed. This node supplies the history it needs; no preceding feedback is visible.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate author prediction: deciding whether a limited negative study can gate referral is the intended competing error; re-review is pending.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: The stated observations distinguish the nearest competing action: Painful weak resisted flexion persists, and neither limited wound inspection nor the ultrasound visualized the wound-level tendon. Counterfactual re-solve: A completely visualized superficial injury with normal painless isolated function could support routine wound care; an adequate specialist study can also guide treatment without being a prerequisite for initial assessment.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Reconciled completed versus limited exploration, supplied an interpretable acquisition limitation, replaced two routine-delay foils with plausible imaging-first gates, and separated this node from earlier teaching. The same repair attempt includes a final label scan: parallel length/category and removal of avoidable key-only noun matching.

case.learningSummary: What it is: A traumatic laceration is a cut through skin or underlying tissue; this pilot's simple form excludes infection, uncontrolled bleeding, and established deeper injury. Typical presentation: The simple phenotype is a recent superficial cut in a stable adult with controlled bleeding and intact distal function. Initial evaluation: Assess mechanism, location, depth, contamination, foreign material concern, and distal tendon and nerve function; separately review wound category and tetanus history. Management in this clinic: Provide basic wound care and routine closure only when the wound is within capability; apply or arrange CDC-supported tetanus prophylaxis. Red flags requiring urgent care: Abnormal active motion, new distal numbness, uncontrolled bleeding, or suspected deeper injury requires higher-level evaluation. Gross contamination requires deliberate cleaning and risk assessment and may exceed clinic capability.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: Four complete product combinations have parallel grammar and equal specificity. No distractor explains its own error or offers antibiotics as an implausible replacement. Review key position is separate from runtime shuffle.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Four active/passive tetanus-prophylaxis combinations.
reasoningSteps: Classify the wound from actual soil contamination rather than its small surface size.
Apply the completed-series interval and check the specific immune exceptions to choose active versus passive protection.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Giving TIG to every dirty wound or overlooking a dirty-wound booster after a completed series.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Soil contamination, a documented complete series, six years since the last dose and no specified immune exception.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: Replace the completed record with an unknown series and both vaccine/TIG become appropriate; a recent dose plus HIV changes the passive-protection decision.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Removing wound category or series timing leaves prophylaxis unresolved. The immune negative is necessary for this exact current CDC exception, not a general reassuring detail.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Prior nodes address tendon assessment and disposition; neither teaches vaccine rules. Immunization pages are newly revealed.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate/hard PGY-2/3 author prediction: Giving TIG to every dirty wound or overlooking a dirty-wound booster after a completed series. No measured difficulty or independent PASS is claimed.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: Resolved using soil contamination, a documented complete series, six years since the last dose and no specified immune exception. The counterfactual was re-solved against every offered option.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Preserved the six-year example and stable tetanus concept while removing explanation-bearing options and abstract adult presentation. The clean-completed-series disputed interval is not used to decide this key.

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Mechanism and depth
items.value: An indoor paper-trimmer blade produced a shallow linear skin cut. The assessment records no puncture tract, soil, saliva or devitalized tissue.

items.label: Vaccine history
items.value: The registry, previous records and patient agree that no tetanus-containing vaccine had ever been received before this encounter.

items.label: Other care
items.value: Cleansing and structural examination were completed.

choices.label: Start the vaccine primary series; no TIG
choices.rationale: The never-vaccinated history establishes an active-vaccine indication without an uncertain recent-dose interval. This clean minor wound does not call for TIG.
choices.temptation: Keep primary immunization and the wound-specific TIG decision separate.
choices.counterfactual: A soil-contaminated puncture in the same unvaccinated patient would call for both vaccine and TIG.

choices.label: Start the vaccine primary series and give TIG
choices.rationale: Active immunization is needed, but lack of previous vaccine does not by itself make TIG appropriate for this wound category.
choices.temptation: Apply the dirty-wound passive-protection rule to all unvaccinated patients.
choices.counterfactual: The same unvaccinated history with a dirty or major wound would support both.

choices.label: Give TIG; do not start the vaccine primary series
choices.rationale: This reverses the decisions: the record establishes a need for active immunization, while the wound does not establish a TIG indication.
choices.temptation: Use temporary antibody as a substitute for primary immunization.
choices.counterfactual: A dirty wound with HIV and a recently completed series can require TIG without another vaccine dose.

choices.label: Give neither vaccine nor TIG
choices.rationale: Low-risk wound status does not remove the independent primary-immunization need.
choices.temptation: Let the wound classification answer both prophylaxis questions.
choices.counterfactual: An appropriately immunized patient with a sufficiently recent dose can need neither product at a wound encounter.

proposals.explanation: Classify the wound from its mechanism and tissue findings, then check the vaccine history separately. This never-vaccinated patient needs active primary immunization. TIG is not indicated for the clean minor wound. Formulation and subsequent valid-dose scheduling remain part of the clinical vaccine plan.

proposals.objective: Interpret an event-related tryptase rise against baseline and separate mast-cell activation from proof of an IgE mechanism.
proposals.currentUpdate: The founder reviews {patientName}'s paired laboratory results after recovery from an interrupted outside anesthetic.
proposals.task: Which interpretation best fits {patientName}'s clinical event and paired tryptase measurements?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Event
items.value: Generalized wheals, wheezing and hypotension developed during induction; emergency treatment was completed before discharge.

items.label: Acute measurement
items.value: Serum tryptase was 7.2 ng/mL in a sample obtained 80 minutes after symptom onset.

items.label: Baseline measurement
items.value: At a well follow-up after recovery, serum tryptase was 3.0 ng/mL. Both reports were marked within their laboratory reference interval.

items.label: Causal assessment
items.value: No agent-specific allergy testing has yet been performed.

choices.label: Mast-cell activation supported; IgE mechanism unresolved
choices.rationale: The event-related value exceeds 1.2 times baseline plus 2 ng/mL: 1.2 x 3.0 + 2 = 5.6. A mediator rise does not by itself identify an IgE mechanism.
choices.temptation: Interpret the paired change and the limit of what it establishes.
choices.counterfactual: A value below the paired criterion would remove this biochemical support, but would not by itself rule out the clinical event.

choices.label: Mast-cell activation unsupported; IgE mechanism unresolved
choices.rationale: The population flag is not the paired comparison. Here 7.2 exceeds 5.6, supporting acute activation in the clinical context.
choices.temptation: Use the normal laboratory flag instead of the individual baseline.
choices.counterfactual: A properly timed result below the paired criterion would not supply this biochemical support.

choices.label: Mast-cell activation supported; IgE mechanism established
choices.rationale: Non-IgE mechanisms can also release mast-cell mediators. Agent-specific clinical evaluation remains necessary.
choices.temptation: Solve the paired comparison but overinterpret mediator release as proof of mechanism.
choices.counterfactual: Concordant specialist exposure assessment and appropriate agent-specific tests may support an IgE-mediated cause.

choices.label: Mast-cell activation unsupported; IgE mechanism established
choices.rationale: This misses the paired rise and assigns a mechanism not established by the displayed record.
choices.temptation: Treat the normal flag as excluding activation while assigning causation from timing alone.
choices.counterfactual: A different full record would need separate evidence for the marker interpretation and causal mechanism.

proposals.explanation: Compare with the patient's baseline: 1.2 x 3.0 + 2 = 5.6 ng/mL; 7.2 exceeds that criterion despite the normal population flag. This supports event-associated mast-cell activation. It identifies neither a culprit nor an IgE mechanism; clinical specialist evaluation is still needed.

proposals.objective: Distinguish a documented material allergy from an unsupported iodine label and apply avoidance across product routes.
proposals.currentUpdate: The founder reviews {patientName}'s specialist findings and a proposed outside procedure plan.
proposals.task: Which preparation and catheter plan best fits {patientName}'s allergy record?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Specialist record
items.value: The previous systemic event was assessed using its chronology and concordant testing. Chlorhexidine allergy was diagnosed.

items.label: Device record
items.value: The proposed antimicrobial catheter coating contains chlorhexidine. An uncoated catheter is also listed.

items.label: Food history
items.value: An iodine-allergy label was added after hives and wheezing from shrimp. The record contains no prior reaction to povidone-iodine.

choices.label: Use povidone-iodine for preparation; select the uncoated catheter
choices.rationale: The food history does not establish povidone-iodine allergy. The chlorhexidine diagnosis also matters to an ingredient on a device, so avoid the coated catheter.
choices.temptation: Resolve the food-label misconception separately from the device ingredient.
choices.counterfactual: A true prior reaction to povidone-iodine would need its own assessment; a coating without the relevant allergen would change the device comparison.

choices.label: Use povidone-iodine for preparation; select the coated catheter
choices.rationale: This rejects an unsupported iodine label but overlooks the established allergen in the coating.
choices.temptation: Treat preparation allergy as relevant only to skin-cleansing bottles.
choices.counterfactual: A different coating without chlorhexidine or another relevant allergen could remove this objection.

choices.label: Defer for povidone-iodine allergy testing; select the uncoated catheter
choices.rationale: The device selection addresses the established risk. Shrimp allergy alone does not justify assigning povidone-iodine allergy or requiring that testing.
choices.temptation: Avoid the known culprit but convert a food label into another product contraindication.
choices.counterfactual: A specific previous reaction to povidone-iodine would justify targeted evaluation.

choices.label: Defer for povidone-iodine allergy testing; select the coated catheter
choices.rationale: This preserves the unsupported food-to-iodine inference while retaining a device carrying the established allergen.
choices.temptation: Accept both the iodine label and a route-limited view of chlorhexidine allergy.
choices.counterfactual: Actual povidone-iodine reaction evidence and a coating without the confirmed allergen would describe a different record.

proposals.explanation: Treat the two records separately. Shrimp allergy does not establish iodine or povidone-iodine allergy. Confirmed chlorhexidine allergy applies to relevant device ingredients as well as preparation solutions. The supported offered plan uses povidone-iodine and the uncoated catheter; a true alternative-product reaction needs its own assessment.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: Removed the explicit avoidance instruction and suitability reassurance. All plans avoid chlorhexidine skin preparation; food-label interpretation now changes whether the plan proceeds. Four balanced combinations prevent convergence.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Four parallel preparation-evaluation and device-selection plans.
reasoningSteps: Interpret the unsupported food-to-iodine label and distinguish it from a true reaction to the proposed preparation.
Apply the confirmed chlorhexidine diagnosis to a non-preparation route, the catheter coating.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Choosing the uncoated device correctly but requiring iodine testing solely because of shrimp allergy.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: The only iodine label comes from a shrimp reaction; chlorhexidine allergy is independently established and the catheter coating contains it.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: A previous povidone-iodine reaction changes preparation assessment; a coating documented without chlorhexidine changes the device choice.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Without food-label provenance, preparation assessment may be necessary. Without the ingredient record, the catheter distinction cannot be resolved.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Standalone clinic chart review. All earlier scored companions are removed. This node supplies the history it needs; no preceding feedback is visible.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate author prediction from two distinct misconception-driven near errors; no claim of universal product tolerability.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: The stated observations distinguish the nearest competing action: The only iodine label comes from a shrimp reaction; chlorhexidine allergy is independently established and the catheter coating contains it. Counterfactual re-solve: A previous povidone-iodine reaction changes preparation assessment; a coating documented without chlorhexidine changes the device choice.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced generic avoidance with two distinct errors: unnecessary preparation-allergy testing and overlooking a device exposure. No universal iodine testing protocol is asserted; testing is a candidate plan being rejected. The same repair attempt includes a final label scan: parallel length/category and removal of avoidable key-only noun matching.

proposals.objective: Use the phenotype and exposure chronology of a new event rather than allow older latex-protein or contact-allergy results to determine its assessment.
proposals.currentUpdate: The founder reviews {patientName}'s resolved outside event alongside the actual earlier allergy reports. Established rubber-chemical precautions remain background care.
proposals.task: Which targeted allergy assessment best addresses {patientName}'s newly documented outside event?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Earlier reports
items.value: Before the new event, serum latex-protein specific IgE was not detected. A later patch assessment of the earlier scaly glove eruption supported a clinically relevant rubber-chemical contact allergy.

items.label: 09:00 record
items.value: Staff wearing natural-rubber gloves applied a tourniquet and handled the forearm before venous access.

items.label: 09:03 record
items.value: Generalized wheals, wheezing and falling blood pressure were documented. The procedure was stopped for emergency care.

items.label: 09:08 record
items.value: Chlorhexidine preparation was first used for venous access during emergency treatment. The patient recovered before the present clinic review.

choices.label: Evaluate current immediate sensitization to latex proteins
choices.rationale: The new phenotype differs from the contact eruption, and natural-rubber exposure preceded it. The old negative assay does not settle a later event. This is a workup target, not proof of a culprit.
choices.temptation: Use phenotype, dated prior assay and exposure order together.
choices.counterfactual: If another plausible immediate allergen preceded symptoms and natural-rubber exposure occurred afterward, that ordering would change the initial target.

choices.label: Evaluate current immediate sensitization to chlorhexidine
choices.rationale: Chlorhexidine is a real immediate allergen, but it was first introduced after this event began. It cannot explain the initial onset in this chronology.
choices.temptation: Select a familiar procedural culprit without reconstructing its actual introduction.
choices.counterfactual: If chlorhexidine had been applied before first symptoms, it could become a relevant specialist-assessment candidate.

choices.label: Repeat delayed patch assessment of rubber chemicals
choices.rationale: The contact allergy remains relevant to background precautions, but repeating that assessment does not address the new rapid multisystem phenotype.
choices.temptation: Let the previous positive test explain every later glove event.
choices.counterfactual: A recurrence limited to delayed eczematous plaques would return emphasis to contact exposures.

proposals.explanation: Preserve the earlier negative latex-protein assay in the history. It does not settle this later event, and the contact-allergy finding addresses a different mechanism. The new phenotype and exposure order support current latex-protein assessment. Chlorhexidine followed onset; the sequence alone does not diagnose a culprit.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: Two choices investigate immediate allergens, so rapid timing no longer uniquely selects an immediate-workup category. All are named specialist assessments. The actual old negative report and chronology are shown.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three targeted specialist allergy assessments.
reasoningSteps: Distinguish the new rapid systemic phenotype from the patch-supported eruption without erasing the prior negative protein assay.
Use exposure chronology to prioritize current assessment rather than the post-onset antiseptic or an already characterized delayed mechanism.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Choosing chlorhexidine, a real immediate procedural allergen, without noticing its first exposure followed symptoms.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: The old protein assay predates this event; natural-rubber exposure precedes the new multisystem findings, while chlorhexidine first appears afterward.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: If chlorhexidine preceded symptoms and natural-rubber exposure followed them, its assessment becomes the appropriate initial candidate. A later purely eczematous recurrence favors contact assessment.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Without timestamps, two immediate candidates remain unresolved. Without the distinct phenotype, contact reassessment may be appropriate.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Standalone clinic chart review. All earlier scored companions are removed. This node supplies the history it needs; no preceding feedback is visible.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate/hard author prediction from mechanism and exposure-order errors; an old negative result remains a real source of reassurance.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: The stated observations distinguish the nearest competing action: The old protein assay predates this event; natural-rubber exposure precedes the new multisystem findings, while chlorhexidine first appears afterward. Counterfactual re-solve: If chlorhexidine preceded symptoms and natural-rubber exposure followed them, its assessment becomes the appropriate initial candidate. A later purely eczematous recurrence favors contact assessment.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Reconciled the negative assay, separated prior teaching, and replaced two delayed-test foils with a chlorhexidine immediate-allergen competitor plus one contact comparator. Culprit uncertainty remains explicit.

proposals.currentUpdate: The founder examines {patientName}'s healed elbow scar and reviews the hand-therapy assessment.
proposals.task: Which reconstructive procedure should be considered for {patientName}'s persistent elbow extension deficit?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Surface
items.value: A narrow firm band remains within the original burn boundary and spans the front of the elbow.

items.label: Movement
items.value: Active and passive extension stop at the same point. The band blanches and tightens during extension; flexion and forearm rotation remain free.

items.label: Therapy course
items.value: Documented stretching and splint use improved strength but did not change the passive endpoint. Imaging shows maintained joint alignment without an osseous block.

choices.label: Scar release with tissue rearrangement
choices.rationale: The skin band and persistent passive tethering identify a functional cutaneous contracture rather than an elevation problem or isolated muscle weakness.
choices.temptation: Localize the limitation using passive movement and skin behavior.
choices.counterfactual: A freely mobile scar with an intra-articular restriction would require another target.

choices.label: Elbow capsular release with arthrolysis
choices.rationale: The visible skin tether is the supported limiting structure; no intra-articular block has been demonstrated.
choices.temptation: Treat every fixed passive endpoint as a joint-capsule problem.
choices.counterfactual: A mobile skin envelope with confirmed capsular contracture could support arthrolysis.

choices.label: Tendon lengthening with adhesiolysis
choices.rationale: The band tightens across the skin and limits passive as well as active movement; the record does not localize the deficit to tendon excursion.
choices.temptation: Infer tendon shortening from an extension deficit without locating the tether.
choices.counterfactual: A deficit localized to tendon shortening with a freely mobile skin envelope would require tendon-focused assessment.

proposals.explanation: The scar's boundary classification does not determine its functional importance. Here the skin band remains a mechanical restraint after therapy, so reconstructive scar release addresses the demonstrated target. The exact rearrangement design requires specialist examination.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: Three operative targets, all specific. The task does not say skin release. Normal alignment does not exclude every capsular disorder; the dynamic skin observation provides the positive localization.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three reconstructive operative targets for the same persistent deficit.
reasoningSteps: Separate a skin tether from joint or tendon limitation using passive motion and the changing band.
Recognize persistent functional restriction after therapy as a reason to consider release rather than cosmetic flattening.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Treating every passive extension deficit as capsular disease or focusing only on whether the scar is raised.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: A blanching cutaneous band at the passive endpoint despite a documented therapy trial.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: A mobile skin envelope with proven capsular restriction changes the operative target.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Delete band behavior and the operative target becomes uncertain. Delete treatment response and timing of escalation is less well supported.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Standalone; not preceded by an explanation that names the release.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate/hard PGY-2/3 author prediction: Treating every passive extension deficit as capsular disease or focusing only on whether the scar is raised. No measured difficulty or independent PASS is claimed.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: Resolved using a blanching cutaneous band at the passive endpoint despite a documented therapy trial. The counterfactual was re-solved against every offered option.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced scar-label recall with mechanical localization and failed conservative treatment. Avoided a fixed maturity-month rule or a specific Z-plasty angle.

proposals.task: Which next diagnostic step best addresses {patientName}'s persistent enlarging nodule?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Clinical course
items.value: A firm nodule at the end of an old scar continues to enlarge and develop surface erosion.

items.label: Acquisition
items.value: A tangential specimen was taken from the nodule itself, not a different scar site. The submitted fragments were shallow crust and surface tissue.

items.label: Microscopy
items.value: Fibrin and superficial granulation tissue were described. Deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue were absent from the submitted specimen.

items.label: Current examination
items.value: The underlying palpable nodule remains after sampling.

choices.label: Obtain a new incisional specimen for histology
choices.rationale: The acquisition did not include tissue needed to assess the palpable lesion. A new adequate sample addresses that limitation; appearance does not establish its diagnosis.
choices.temptation: Distinguish limited acquisition from inadequate slide review.
choices.counterfactual: If a representative full-depth specimen existed, additional levels or specialist review could address an interpretive discrepancy.

choices.label: Request additional sections from the current specimen
choices.rationale: Additional levels cannot add anatomical tissue that was not acquired. Only superficial material was submitted while the palpable lesion remains.
choices.temptation: Treat a missing tissue compartment as a microscopy-level problem.
choices.counterfactual: Levels may help when the necessary tissue is present in the block but not represented on the reviewed sections.

choices.label: Request specialist review of the current specimen
choices.rationale: Expert review can clarify interpretation, but cannot identify deeper lesional tissue absent from the material.
choices.temptation: Seek more authoritative interpretation of a sample lacking the target depth.
choices.counterfactual: Review is useful when a representative specimen and the clinical findings appear discordant.

proposals.explanation: The sampled location was correct; its depth was not adequate for the remaining nodule. Distinguish missing tissue from a need for more sections or another interpretation. Obtain an adequate deeper biopsy before scar-directed treatment. This does not diagnose a particular malignancy.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: Every option investigates the actual lesion; no wrong-site repetition selects the key. No option is labelled representative or definitive. Acquisition depth must be distinguished from sectioning depth.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three next tissue-diagnosis steps.
reasoningSteps: Interpret acquisition and pathology as a depth problem despite sampling the correct lesion.
Choose new tissue acquisition rather than further work on material lacking the required compartment.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Requesting deeper levels, a legitimate pathology tool, when the needed anatomical tissue is absent.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Only shallow crust and surface tissue were submitted, while the enlarging palpable nodule remains and deep dermis is absent.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: If a representative full-depth specimen were available but its interpretation were discordant, additional levels or a second review could be better.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Without specimen depth, additional levels are reasonable. Without the remaining palpable nodule, repeating acquisition is less well established.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Standalone clinic chart review. All earlier scored companions are removed. This node supplies the history it needs; no preceding feedback is visible.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate/hard author prediction: plausible confusion between deeper sections and deeper tissue acquisition.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: The stated observations distinguish the nearest competing action: Only shallow crust and surface tissue were submitted, while the enlarging palpable nodule remains and deep dermis is absent. Counterfactual re-solve: If a representative full-depth specimen were available but its interpretation were discordant, additional levels or a second review could be better.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced the opposite-scar-site mismatch with a same-lesion sampling limitation and two credible pathology steps. Verified repeat biopsy for inadequate sampling in the AAD guideline; no method is claimed universally optimal. The same repair attempt includes a final label scan: parallel length/category and removal of avoidable key-only noun matching. Removed a remaining avoidable literal noun echo while retaining the clinical monitoring or acquisition information.

items.label: Change in the skin paddle
items.value: The previously soft paddle became tense and violaceous. After pressure, color returned almost immediately; pinprick produced brisk dark blood.

items.label: Native limb findings
items.value: The ipsilateral digits remained warm with palpable distal pulses.

items.label: Monitoring
items.value: The flap's recorded arterial signal was still audible. The record had not yet established a surgically correctable lesion or excluded one.

choices.label: Proceed to urgent microsurgical pedicle exploration
choices.rationale: Combined flap findings suggest threatened local outflow despite persistent inflow and native perfusion. Assess a correctable pedicle problem before nonoperative salvage.
choices.temptation: Localize the threat before assuming an adjunct can correct the pedicle.
choices.counterfactual: After exploration excludes or corrects a remediable obstruction, selected temporary offloading may be considered.

choices.label: Obtain native-limb arterial angiography before exploration
choices.rationale: The leading concern is localized to the flap while native perfusion remains present. This makes another study a prerequisite for exploration of a potentially correctable flap problem.
choices.temptation: Mislocalize threatened transferred tissue to native-limb arterial occlusion.
choices.counterfactual: New loss of native pulses or a cold ipsilateral limb raises another supply concern requiring urgent specialist assessment.

choices.label: Start medicinal-leech offloading before exploration
choices.rationale: Offloading does not correct a mechanical pedicle problem. A surgically remediable cause remains unassessed.
choices.temptation: Recognize an outflow phenotype but apply later salvage at the wrong stage.
choices.counterfactual: After appropriate surgical assessment excludes or corrects a remediable lesion, temporary offloading may be considered by the microsurgical team.

proposals.explanation: Use skin findings and ipsilateral circulation together: a tense violaceous paddle with brisk dark bleeding suggests threatened flap outflow. Urgent microsurgical exploration addresses a potentially remediable pedicle problem. An arterial sound does not guarantee tissue perfusion, and leeches do not repair an obstructed pedicle.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: The task does not preselect an operation, and no venous monitoring label supplies the answer. Exploration and offloading both address the apparent threat, so localization alone does not settle management.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three urgent next management paths.
reasoningSteps: Localize deterioration to flap outflow using raw skin and ipsilateral findings without naming a particular thrombus.
Choose urgent exploration before offloading because a correctable mechanical cause remains unassessed.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Recognizing outflow compromise but starting leeches before excluding a correctable pedicle problem.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: The tense violaceous paddle has brisk dark bleeding; native digits remain perfused and mechanical causes have not been assessed.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: Correction or exclusion of a remediable obstruction changes the stage at which offloading may be considered. New native distal ischemia changes localization and priorities.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Without the prior-assessment status, exploration versus adjunct is unresolved. Without local and ipsilateral findings, the native arterial competitor is harder to separate.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Standalone clinic chart review. All earlier scored companions are removed. This node supplies the history it needs; no preceding feedback is visible.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate/hard author prediction from localization plus treatment-stage selection; no exact salvage deadline or outcome probability.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: The stated observations distinguish the nearest competing action: The tense violaceous paddle has brisk dark bleeding; native digits remain perfused and mechanical causes have not been assessed. Counterfactual re-solve: Correction or exclusion of a remediable obstruction changes the stage at which offloading may be considered. New native distal ischemia changes localization and priorities.

items.label: Earlier examination
items.value: The flap was soft and pink; arterial and venous monitoring signals were present.

items.value: The flap became swollen and purple, with rapid refill and dark bleeding on pinprick. The arterial signal persisted; the venous signal changed.

answerChoices.label: Explore the venous anastomosis and drainage pedicle
answerChoices.rationale: The local congested pattern despite maintained inflow directs urgent exploration toward venous outflow; a persistent arterial signal is not proof of a complete circuit.

answerChoices.rationale: The recorded rapid dark bleeding and swelling are more consistent with impaired drainage than isolated loss of inflow.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The recorded rapid dark bleeding and swelling are more consistent with impaired drainage than isolated loss of inflow.

answerChoices.label: Explore proximal arterial supply to the entire limb
answerChoices.rationale: Stable systemic pressure, preserved flap inflow and a warm opposite limb do not support a generalized inflow failure as the explanation for the local congested flap.

answerChoices.label: Complete blood count with hemoglobin trend

answerChoices.label: Evacuate interface fluid and resecure the existing graft
answerChoices.rationale: The new barrier needs correction, while the tissue findings support an attempt to retain the graft rather than excise it. Continued assessment is required; one sign does not guarantee survival.

answerChoices.label: Evacuate interface fluid and replace the lifted graft segment
answerChoices.rationale: This addresses the barrier but discards tissue for which the record still describes perfusion. The observations do not establish segmental necrosis.

answerChoices.rationale: External fixation does not remove the fluid already separating the sheet from its bed.

decisionNodes.explanation: Read the interface and the graft separately. A new fluid layer interrupts contact, but detachment alone does not establish necrosis.
