case.learningSummary: What it is: A traumatic laceration is a cut through skin or underlying tissue; this pilot's simple form excludes infection, uncontrolled bleeding, and established deeper injury. Typical presentation: The simple phenotype is a recent superficial cut in a stable adult with controlled bleeding and intact distal function. Initial evaluation: Assess mechanism, location, depth, contamination, foreign material concern, and distal tendon and nerve function; separately review wound category and tetanus history. Management in this clinic: Provide basic wound care and routine closure only when the wound is within capability; apply or arrange CDC-supported tetanus prophylaxis. Red flags requiring urgent care: Abnormal active motion, new distal numbness, uncontrolled bleeding, or suspected deeper injury requires higher-level evaluation. Gross contamination requires deliberate cleaning and risk assessment and may exceed clinic capability.

choices.label: Tetanus-containing vaccine and TIG

choices.label: Tetanus-containing vaccine; no TIG

choices.label: Neither tetanus-containing vaccine nor TIG
choices.rationale: The actual record does not establish the completed recent series needed for that conclusion.

choices.counterfactual: A completed recent series with no specified immune exception could support neither product.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: The full four-combination set prevents component novelty or majority logic. History uncertainty is actual evidence status, not an odd qualifier appended to the key. No dose is fabricated.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Four active/passive prophylaxis combinations.
reasoningSteps: Recognize a contaminated puncture as a dirty/major wound.
Interpret the incomplete evidence of a primary series and distinguish active from passive protection.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Counting one remembered dose as a complete series and selecting a vaccine-only booster plan.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: A soil-contaminated puncture with only one recorded vaccine dose and no established completed series.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: An otherwise identical clean minor wound changes the TIG decision; documentation of a completed series also changes the pathway.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Delete the record limitation and a completed-series pathway might apply. Delete the contamination and TIG is no longer established.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Standalone alternative tetanus variant; no other tetanus answer is an earlier scored companion.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate/hard PGY-2/3 author prediction: Counting one remembered dose as a complete series and selecting a vaccine-only booster plan. No measured difficulty or independent PASS is claimed.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: Resolved using a soil-contaminated puncture with only one recorded vaccine dose and no established completed series. The counterfactual was re-solved against every offered option.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed the antibiotics-only caricature and the generic assess-everything key. This is a moderate application variant; immune-exception variants provide the harder counterpoint.

choices.label: TIG; no tetanus-containing vaccine
choices.rationale: Current CDC guidance calls for TIG in a dirty wound with HIV regardless of prior immunization; the recent completed series does not require another vaccine dose.
choices.temptation: Apply the immune exception to passive protection while preserving the recent-dose vaccine rule.
choices.counterfactual: Without HIV or severe immunodeficiency, the same recent completed series could support neither product.

choices.label: Neither tetanus-containing vaccine nor TIG
choices.rationale: The recent completed series addresses the vaccine decision but does not override the HIV TIG exception.
choices.temptation: Stop the assessment once the vaccination record is reassuring.
choices.counterfactual: The same dirty wound with a recent completed series and no specified immune exception can need neither.

choices.label: Tetanus-containing vaccine and TIG
choices.rationale: HIV establishes a TIG indication here; it does not create a need to repeat a completed-series vaccine dose from two years earlier.
choices.temptation: Correctly add passive protection but also restart active protection without an indication.
choices.counterfactual: An incomplete series in this dirty wound would support both products.

choices.label: Tetanus-containing vaccine; no TIG
choices.rationale: This repeats an unnecessary vaccine while omitting the passive protection specifically indicated by the wound and HIV history.
choices.temptation: Treat immune status as a reason for an extra booster rather than check the actual TIG guidance.
choices.counterfactual: A completed series with a longer dirty-wound booster interval and no immune exception can call for vaccine without TIG.

reviewedProposals.explanation: Check the two prophylaxis decisions separately. HIV is a specified CDC exception requiring TIG for dirty/major wounds regardless of immunization history. reasoningSteps: Interpret the recent completed series as adequate for the vaccine-dose question.

manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: A dirty puncture in a person with HIV whose complete series was boosted two years earlier.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: Removing HIV/severe immunodeficiency changes the best combination to neither; an incomplete series changes it to both.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Delete HIV and the TIG key changes. Delete the recent completed record and vaccine necessity becomes unresolved.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Standalone higher-difficulty variant; earlier tetanus feedback is not part of its visible context.

items.label: Intake
items.value: The diary records tea, plain rice, bread and small portions of meat, with almost no fruit or vegetables over the preceding months.

items.label: Examination
items.value: The wound is slow to granulate. Gingival bleeding and scattered petechiae and easy bruising are present.

items.label: Other findings
items.value: Platelet count and routine coagulation studies are within their laboratory reference ranges.

choices.label: Plasma vitamin C concentration
choices.rationale: The restricted intake with connective-tissue and perifollicular bleeding signs supports targeted assessment of ascorbate status.
choices.temptation: Integrate dietary exposure with the pattern of tissue fragility rather than slow healing alone.
choices.counterfactual: A clinically supported zinc-deficiency pattern would instead justify targeted zinc assessment.

choices.label: Serum zinc concentration
choices.rationale: Zinc deficiency can impair healing, but the supplied diet and gingival/capillary-fragility bleeding pattern more directly support an ascorbate question.
choices.temptation: Choose a familiar wound-healing micronutrient without matching the accompanying phenotype.
choices.counterfactual: A clinically compatible zinc-deficiency phenotype and nutritional assessment could justify zinc testing.

choices.label: Repeat prothrombin time and INR
choices.rationale: The current tests do not show a routine coagulation abnormality; the combination of diet and tissue-fragility signs remains unexplained by repeating them.
choices.temptation: Treat every bleeding sign as a vitamin-K/coagulation-factor problem.
choices.counterfactual: A newly prolonged coagulation result or relevant anticoagulant exposure could justify a coagulation-focused assessment.

reviewedProposals.explanation: Slow healing is nonspecific. The dietary pattern plus gingival and cutaneous bleeding makes targeted ascorbate assessment appropriate here. This does not establish a supplement dose or a benefit from high-dose vitamin C in replete postoperative patients; broader nutrition prescriptions remain in the nutrition topic.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: Three named laboratory investigations with the same timing profile. No supplied scurvy diagnosis, cofactor name or advertised supplement. The key is not longer than its distractors.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three current laboratory investigations.
reasoningSteps: Interpret intake and the distribution of bleeding as a connective-tissue deficiency pattern despite routine coagulation tests.
Select a targeted status investigation rather than repeat an unrevealing coagulation study or choose a wound nutrient by association.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Recommending wound supplements or a zinc assay from slow healing while ignoring the associated dietary/bleeding pattern.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Restricted fruit/vegetable intake with gingival and cutaneous bleeding and normal routine coagulation studies.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: A different compatible deficiency phenotype changes the nutritional test; newly abnormal coagulation studies change the priority.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Delete bleeding distribution and impaired healing alone cannot prioritize vitamin C. Delete the diet and the deficiency explanation is less strongly localized. Normal coagulation is needed for the competing factor-pathway interpretation.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Standalone. No approved vitamin-C recall item is a preceding companion that gives this answer.

manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced the weak no-deficiency versus high-dose counseling comparison with a positive targeted evaluation problem. New clinical meaning has a new concept identity; the old approved hydroxylation cards are retained exactly.

items.label: Prior reaction
items.value: An itchy vesicular eruption appeared after the procedure and followed the rectangular outline of the adhesive dressing, extending beyond the incision. There was no purulent drainage or systemic illness.

items.label: Exposure comparison
items.value: A separate site prepared with the same antiseptic but covered with gauze did not develop the eruption.

items.label: Recovery
items.value: The eruption resolved after dressing removal and local treatment; the patient is well today.

choices.label: Patch testing to relevant dressing and adhesive allergens
choices.rationale: The delayed eczematous contact pattern calls for an exposure-directed contact-allergy evaluation, not a test of immediate mast-cell activation.
choices.temptation: Combine timing, morphology and exposure geography without declaring a specific culprit from appearance.
choices.counterfactual: Rapid hives, bronchospasm and hypotension after exposure would require an immediate-hypersensitivity evaluation instead.

choices.label: Serum specific-IgE testing to immediate latex allergens
choices.rationale: That pathway evaluates immediate latex-protein sensitization rather than the delayed dressing-footprint eruption recorded here.
choices.temptation: Use the word allergy as a reason to select an IgE assay regardless of phenotype.
choices.counterfactual: An immediate latex-linked systemic reaction could support latex-specific testing under allergy supervision.

choices.label: Paired serum tryptase testing around the next procedure
choices.rationale: Tryptase addresses a systemic mast-cell event, not retrospective identification of a delayed contact allergen. A new exposure should not be created merely to capture a marker.
choices.temptation: Confuse a systemic reaction marker with delayed-allergen identification.
choices.counterfactual: If an actual systemic perioperative reaction occurs, acute and baseline samples can support its assessment.

reviewedProposals.explanation: The pattern supports evaluating delayed contact sensitization and selecting relevant patch-test materials. The footprint does not prove which ingredient caused the event; specialist testing and clinical relevance are still required.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: Three named allergy investigations; all have timing estimates. No supplied allergic-contact diagnosis or type-IV label. The task does not uniquely match the patch-test option with a mechanism word.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three allergy investigations before the next procedure.
reasoningSteps: Interpret delayed vesicular dermatitis in relation to the actual dressing distribution and comparison site.
Choose contact-allergen testing rather than immediate allergy markers.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Ordering an IgE or mast-cell test for every postoperative allergy label.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Delayed vesicular eruption limited to the dressing footprint with a same-preparation uncovered comparison site.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: Immediate respiratory/circulatory symptoms after latex exposure would change the testing pathway.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Delete timing/morphology and an immediate pathway becomes harder to exclude. Delete the exposure map and the relevant contact-testing panel is less focused.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: First node. Later patch-test results and material-selection options are hidden.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate/hard PGY-2/3 author prediction: Ordering an IgE or mast-cell test for every postoperative allergy label. No measured difficulty or independent PASS is claimed.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: Resolved using delayed vesicular eruption limited to the dressing footprint with a same-preparation uncovered comparison site. The counterfactual was re-solved against every offered option.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed the original specialist-confirmed diagnosis that made mechanism classification trivial. Kept necessary absence of systemic illness without using an antibiotic-treatment foil.

choices.label: Retain a perioperative hypersensitivity workup
choices.rationale: The multisystem clinical event remains concerning despite an acute value inside the population interval; the paired record and exposure history still need specialist evaluation.
choices.temptation: Distinguish a reference interval from a definitive exclusion test.
choices.counterfactual: An isolated predictable medication effect with no supporting systemic allergic features could lead to a different workup.

choices.label: Classify the event as anesthetic vasodilation
choices.rationale: A normal acute marker does not explain away hives and wheezing accompanying hypotension.
choices.temptation: Use one normal result to substitute a common physiologic anesthetic effect for the whole event.
choices.counterfactual: Isolated hypotension after induction without skin or respiratory findings may support a nonallergic physiologic explanation.

choices.label: Classify the event as proven drug-specific IgE allergy
choices.rationale: Even a mast-cell event does not identify the culprit or prove an IgE mechanism from this record.
choices.temptation: Correctly suspect anaphylaxis but overstate what the biomarker and timing establish.
choices.counterfactual: A specialist's concordant exposure history and validated culprit-specific assessment may support an IgE-mediated diagnosis.

reviewedProposals.explanation: The clinical event still warrants evaluation. A population-normal acute tryptase neither rules out the event nor identifies a drug-specific IgE mechanism. Interpret the actual paired record in its clinical context.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: Three interpretations of the event, with similar scope. The key does not assert the diagnosis or culprit. Neither the task nor header says confirmed IgE or type I.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three interpretations guiding the same post-event workup.
reasoningSteps: Interpret a multisystem perioperative event rather than a single blood-pressure change.

manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Hives and wheeze accompany hypotension despite a population-normal acute marker.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: Isolated expected hypotension without skin or respiratory features could favor anesthetic vasodilation.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Delete the systemic event and a routine physiologic explanation becomes credible. Delete the normal marker and the specific evidence-limit trap disappears.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: First node. No later culprit-test results are visible.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate/hard PGY-2/3 author prediction: Treating a normal acute tryptase as an exclusion test, or treating concern for anaphylaxis as proof of IgE causality. No measured difficulty or independent PASS is claimed.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: Resolved using hives and wheeze accompany hypotension despite a population-normal acute marker. The counterfactual was re-solved against every offered option.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed the supplied type-I/IgE diagnosis and four recall-label options. Re-solved both over-exclusion and over-attribution errors; no diagnostic formula or invented sampling interval.

reviewedProposals.task: Which investigation should be arranged for {patientName}'s recurrent glove-associated skin problem?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Pattern
items.value: Itchy scaly plaques develop after repeated wear and persist between glove sessions. There have been no immediate wheals, respiratory symptoms or faintness.

items.label: Glove history
items.value: Similar plaques occurred with natural-rubber gloves and with a nitrile replacement.

items.label: Previous testing
items.value: Serum latex-protein specific IgE was negative; the product rubber chemicals were not tested.

choices.label: Rubber-chemical and glove-material patch testing
choices.rationale: A delayed persistent eczema pattern across different rubber products warrants assessment of shared chemical contact allergens, rather than assuming the nitrile label excludes allergy.
choices.temptation: Combine the reaction phenotype with the shared product exposures and the scope of the prior test.
choices.counterfactual: An immediate systemic latex-protein reaction would require a different specialist testing pathway.

choices.label: Repeat serum latex-protein specific-IgE testing
choices.rationale: Repeating the same immediate-protein test does not assess the untested delayed rubber-chemical pathway suggested by this course.
choices.temptation: Treat a negative latex assay as incomplete only because symptoms continue, without checking what it measures.
choices.counterfactual: A new immediate latex-linked event could warrant an immediate allergy reassessment.

choices.label: Immediate latex-protein skin-prick testing
choices.rationale: This is an immediate protein-sensitization investigation, whereas the persistent eczematous pattern raises a different immune and exposure question.
choices.temptation: Select a different format of the same mismatched pathway.
choices.counterfactual: Immediate urticaria or systemic symptoms after latex exposure could justify supervised protein testing.

reviewedProposals.explanation: A negative immediate latex-protein assay does not evaluate all glove reactions. The persistent delayed eczema and reactions to more than one rubber product support exposure-directed patch testing for relevant manufacturing chemicals.

reasoningSteps: Interpret a persistent delayed eczematous course rather than an immediate protein reaction.
Recognize the prior assay's scope and select testing that can assess shared rubber chemicals.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Concluding that nitrile use or a negative latex-protein IgE test excludes glove allergy.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Persistent delayed plaques with both rubber and nitrile products and no chemical patch testing.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: Immediate hives with bronchospasm after latex would change the workup to immediate hypersensitivity testing.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Delete the phenotype and an immediate pathway becomes plausible. Delete product/test scope and repeating latex testing is harder to reject.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: First node; the specific positive chemical result is not yet visible.

manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced supplied type-IV diagnosis and cell-name recall with a scope mismatch between the actual prior test and exposure phenotype.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: Three named specialist testing pathways with equal timing scope. No pre-answer type-I diagnosis or instruction that a latex protein caused the event. The old positive result is deliberately true and must be used within its scope.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three specialist diagnostic-testing pathways.
reasoningSteps: Compare the old delayed eczematous course with the new rapid multisystem event.
Select the matching immediate-allergy investigation rather than repeat a valid but different contact test.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Anchoring on a true earlier contact-allergy result and assigning it to a different later reaction.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: New rapid wheals, wheezing and hypotension compared with earlier persistent scaly plaques.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: If the later event instead repeated delayed plaques, targeted contact/product patch assessment would be appropriate.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Delete the interval phenotype change and repeating patch assessment could be appropriate. Delete the old valid result and the anchoring error disappears.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Earlier feedback concerns a delayed eruption and does not establish the new event. The later findings are revealed only now; no immediate-event diagnosis is supplied by a preceding answer.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate/hard PGY-2/3 author prediction: Anchoring on a true earlier contact-allergy result and assigning it to a different later reaction. No measured difficulty or independent PASS is claimed.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: Resolved using new rapid wheals, wheezing and hypotension compared with earlier persistent scaly plaques. The counterfactual was re-solved against every offered option.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced the first draft's ingredient-letter matching exercise after the manual cue attack showed that it was solvable without interpreting a new clinical event. Re-solved the new mechanism-versus-test mismatch.

items.label: Surface
items.value: A narrow firm band remains within the original burn boundary and spans the front of the elbow.

items.label: Movement
items.value: Active and passive extension stop at the same point. The band blanches and tightens during extension; flexion and forearm rotation remain free.

items.label: Therapy course
items.value: Documented stretching and splint use improved strength but did not change the passive endpoint. Imaging shows maintained joint alignment without an osseous block.

choices.label: Scar release with tissue rearrangement
choices.rationale: The skin band and persistent passive tethering identify a functional cutaneous contracture rather than an elevation problem or isolated muscle weakness.
choices.temptation: Localize the limitation using passive movement and skin behavior.
choices.counterfactual: A freely mobile scar with an intra-articular restriction would require another target.

choices.label: Elbow capsular release with arthrolysis
choices.rationale: The visible skin tether is the supported limiting structure; no intra-articular block has been demonstrated.
choices.temptation: Treat every fixed passive endpoint as a joint-capsule problem.
choices.counterfactual: A mobile skin envelope with confirmed capsular contracture could support arthrolysis.

choices.label: Tendon lengthening with adhesiolysis
choices.rationale: The band tightens across the skin and limits passive as well as active movement; the record does not localize the deficit to tendon excursion.
choices.temptation: Infer tendon shortening from an extension deficit without locating the tether.
choices.counterfactual: A deficit localized to tendon shortening with a freely mobile skin envelope would require tendon-focused assessment.

reviewedProposals.explanation: The scar's boundary classification does not determine its functional importance. Here the skin band remains a mechanical restraint after therapy, so reconstructive scar release addresses the demonstrated target. The exact rearrangement design requires specialist examination.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: Three operative targets, all specific. The task does not say skin release. Normal alignment does not exclude every capsular disorder; the dynamic skin observation provides the positive localization.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three reconstructive operative targets for the same persistent deficit.
reasoningSteps: Separate a skin tether from joint or tendon limitation using passive motion and the changing band.
Recognize persistent functional restriction after therapy as a reason to consider release rather than cosmetic flattening.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Treating every passive extension deficit as capsular disease or focusing only on whether the scar is raised.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: A blanching cutaneous band at the passive endpoint despite a documented therapy trial.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: A mobile skin envelope with proven capsular restriction changes the operative target.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Delete band behavior and the operative target becomes uncertain. Delete treatment response and timing of escalation is less well supported.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Standalone; not preceded by an explanation that names the release.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate/hard PGY-2/3 author prediction: Treating every passive extension deficit as capsular disease or focusing only on whether the scar is raised. No measured difficulty or independent PASS is claimed.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: Resolved using a blanching cutaneous band at the passive endpoint despite a documented therapy trial. The counterfactual was re-solved against every offered option.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced scar-label recall with mechanical localization and failed conservative treatment. Avoided a fixed maturity-month rule or a specific Z-plasty angle.

assertions.text: Localize a fixed movement deficit to scar tethering before choosing the surgical target.

The scar's boundary classification does not determine its functional importance. Here the skin band remains a mechanical restraint after therapy, so reconstructive scar release addresses the demonstrated target. The exact rearrangement design requires specialist examination.
Scar release with tissue rearrangement
The skin band and persistent passive tethering identify a functional cutaneous contracture rather than an elevation problem or isolated muscle weakness.
A freely mobile scar with an intra-articular restriction would require another target.
Elbow capsular release with arthrolysis
The visible skin tether is the supported limiting structure; no intra-articular block has been demonstrated.
A mobile skin envelope with confirmed capsular contracture could support arthrolysis.
Tendon lengthening with adhesiolysis
The band tightens across the skin and limits passive as well as active movement; the record does not localize the deficit to tendon excursion.
A deficit localized to tendon shortening with a freely mobile skin envelope would require tendon-focused assessment.

items.label: Morphology
items.value: Firm smooth tissue extends beyond the recorded incision footprint. The skin surface is fully closed, without a separate growing nodule or ulcer.

items.label: Treatment response
items.value: Silicone gel was used as directed through a documented course. It reduced surface dryness but the thick central portion remains tender and catches on clothing.

items.label: Function
items.value: Shoulder and elbow motion are full; the skin moves freely over the deeper tissues.

choices.label: Intralesional triamcinolone injection course
choices.rationale: A symptomatic raised pathological scar has persisted despite surface therapy, while no contracture or separate suspicious lesion directs another procedure.
choices.temptation: Distinguish treatment of active scar bulk from skin dryness or a mechanical tether.
choices.counterfactual: A true fixed contracture would call for functional reconstruction rather than injection as the whole plan.

choices.label: Further topical silicone gel treatment
choices.rationale: The recorded response did not address the persistent painful central bulk; repeating the same treatment does not respond to that residual problem.
choices.temptation: Treat improved dryness as evidence that the clinically important symptoms are controlled.
choices.counterfactual: A mild improving scar with controlled symptoms could reasonably continue silicone treatment.

choices.label: Scar release with tissue rearrangement
choices.rationale: Full motion and a mobile skin envelope do not establish a functional contracture that would justify release.
choices.temptation: Equate a thick painful scar with a mechanical movement deficit.
choices.counterfactual: A scar band causing fixed functional restriction despite therapy could support release.

reviewedProposals.explanation: The current problem is painful persistent scar bulk rather than dryness or joint tethering. Intralesional triamcinolone is a supported option. This item does not claim that it universally outranks every other scar therapy or prescribe a dose.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: Three named local scar interventions. The key is concise rather than uniquely comprehensive. No treatment mechanism is announced in the task. Necessary normal mobility distinguishes a real release indication.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three local scar-treatment plans at the same visit.
reasoningSteps: Infer pathological scar overgrowth and identify the residual symptom after a real treatment course.
Choose treatment directed at scar bulk rather than repeat the component that improved or operate for an absent functional tether.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Confusing improved surface dryness with control of the symptomatic scar, or treating thickness as contracture.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Persistent tender raised bulk after silicone despite freely mobile skin and full joint motion.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: If pain and bulk were steadily resolving, continuing silicone would be reasonable; fixed passive restriction would support reconstructive release.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Deleting the response makes repeat silicone harder to rank. Deleting the functional examination leaves a meaningful possible indication for release.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Standalone: no prior definition task names the lesion or its treatment.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate/hard PGY-2/3 author prediction: Confusing improved surface dryness with control of the symptomatic scar, or treating thickness as contracture. No measured difficulty or independent PASS is claimed.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: Resolved using persistent tender raised bulk after silicone despite freely mobile skin and full joint motion. The counterfactual was re-solved against every offered option.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed atrophic and flat-scar foils from a treatment task and replaced them with actual care alternatives. Exact modality choice remains a clinician question; no claimed gold-standard treatment.

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Prior operations
items.value: Two excisions were followed by primary closure and routine wound care. The removed tissue showed keloidal scar.

items.label: Current course
items.value: The lesion has regrown beyond each old incision. Intralesional steroid treatment gave temporary shrinkage followed by symptomatic regrowth.

items.label: Current lesion
items.value: A discrete earlobe mass is present without ulceration; the consultation concerns another excision after the documented recurrences.

choices.label: Excision with planned adjuvant radiotherapy
choices.rationale: For a selected recurrent adult keloid, another excision requires a recurrence-reduction strategy; specialist guidance supports planned adjuvant treatment.
choices.temptation: Use the repeated recurrence pattern rather than assume a different closure creates a cure.
choices.counterfactual: A mild lesion responding to nonsurgical treatment may not warrant another operation; radiotherapy suitability also requires specialist and patient review.

choices.label: Excision with a wider normal-skin margin
choices.rationale: Increasing excision extent does not substitute for addressing the tendency of this repeatedly recurrent scar to regrow.
choices.temptation: Treat keloid recurrence as an oncologic margin-clearance problem.
choices.counterfactual: A pathology-confirmed neoplasm can require disease-specific oncologic margins, a different diagnosis and topic.

choices.label: Excision with full-thickness skin-graft coverage
choices.rationale: Changing coverage can address a tissue defect but does not by itself provide the planned recurrence prevention missing from the prior excisions.
choices.temptation: Treat graft coverage as an intrinsic cure for keloid biology.
choices.counterfactual: A residual defect unsuitable for direct closure may require a graft as part of a broader specialist plan.

reviewedProposals.explanation: Repeated histologically confirmed keloid recurrence is not solved simply by making an excision wider or changing the covering skin. If another excision is selected, planned adjunctive treatment must be part of the discussion. Specialist radiotherapy suitability and alternatives remain for exact clinician review.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: All labels are excision plans of comparable length. No alone wording or generic multidisciplinary answer. The question does not say radiation prevents recurrence. Prior steroid response is meaningful treatment evidence, not a blanket exclusion of conservative care.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three surgical plans at the same re-excision consultation.
reasoningSteps: Interpret repeated growth beyond prior incisions as recurrent scar biology rather than inadequate cancer margins.
Compare the proposed operations for a planned recurrence-reduction component after prior treatment failure.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Escalating excision margins or changing coverage while leaving recurrence prevention unaddressed.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Two confirmed keloid recurrences after excision/primary closure and only temporary response to local steroid.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: An improving mild lesion would favor ongoing nonsurgical care; a neoplasm would require a different margin-directed plan.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Delete prior pathology and a tumor mimic remains possible. Delete recurrences and the rationale for specialist combined re-excision weakens. Do not turn this selected plan into a general mandate for all keloids.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Standalone; no earlier feedback supplies the surgical adjunct answer.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate/hard PGY-2/3 author prediction: Escalating excision margins or changing coverage while leaving recurrence prevention unaddressed. No measured difficulty or independent PASS is claimed.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: Resolved using two confirmed keloid recurrences after excision/primary closure and only temporary response to local steroid. The counterfactual was re-solved against every offered option.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced flat/atrophic distractors with actual procedural errors. Preserved NHS general caution versus specialist combined-treatment scope as an explicit clinician decision; no radiation dose, schedule or risk threshold authored.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: No option is serial observation. All are specific rescue interventions. The record supplies actual exploration findings instead of declaring surgery impossible; a surgeon's absence of a suitable vessel is necessary technical evidence, not a general permission cue.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three adjunctive/rescue strategies after the same completed operation.
reasoningSteps: Interpret persistent distal congestion in the setting of a patent revised pedicle rather than assume repeated anastomotic failure.
Use the residual small-vessel problem and response to surface release to select temporary offloading.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Automatically repeat exploration after the anastomotic problem has been corrected, or substitute oxygen for drainage.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Patent revised drainage, diffuse distal small-vein injury and a small paddle that softens with surface release.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: A newly thrombosed drainage anastomosis or an additional usable venous target changes the priority to surgical correction.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Delete the exploration result and urgent revision may outrank leeches. Delete the compartment/response evidence and diffuse failure or poor inflow remains unresolved.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Prior feedback localizes an urgent outflow problem but does not name nonsurgical salvage. New operative results change the remaining decision.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate/hard PGY-2/3 author prediction: Automatically repeat exploration after the anastomotic problem has been corrected, or substitute oxygen for drainage. No measured difficulty or independent PASS is claimed.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: Resolved using patent revised drainage, diffuse distal small-vein injury and a small paddle that softens with surface release. The counterfactual was re-solved against every offered option.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Moved the held v3 objective to a later salvage phase with an operative target assessment. Directly verified exploration priority and leech limitations; old source holds remain historical and are not silently closed.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: Three investigations, all with timing proposals. No wait preview is unique to the key. The task names symptoms rather than anemia. The medication observation distinguishes the INR temptation without ruling out every systemic cause.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three current diagnostic investigations for the new symptoms.
reasoningSteps: Recognize that improved paddle color can coexist with treatment-related external blood loss.
Choose a hemoglobin assessment for the new systemic problem instead of another local-flow study or an indirect coagulation measure.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Using visible flap improvement as reassurance about the whole patient.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Ongoing treated-site bleeding with new orthostatic symptoms while the paddle improves.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: With a new cool pale flap and lost signal but no blood-loss symptoms, urgent vascular reassessment would take priority.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Delete the bleeding/systemic row and hemoglobin cannot be prioritized. Delete local improvement and simultaneous flap failure could change urgency and order.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Earlier feedback explains venous drainage but deliberately does not rehearse systemic blood loss or monitoring. This is a distinct safety decision, not another congestion label.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate/hard PGY-2/3 author prediction: Using visible flap improvement as reassurance about the whole patient. No measured difficulty or independent PASS is claimed.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: Resolved using ongoing treated-site bleeding with new orthostatic symptoms while the paddle improves. The counterfactual was re-solved against every offered option.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed numeric blood-loss estimates, transfusion cutoffs and a weak wait-and-see choice. These are future/planned hospital investigations, not executed clinic orders.

decisionNodes.stem: Which intervention should have been prioritized for the new collection beneath {patientName}'s sheet graft?

answerChoices.label: Evacuate the collection and resecure the graft
answerChoices.rationale: The localized fluid barrier is a potentially reversible interruption of contact, rather than proof that the whole reconstruction must be replaced.

answerChoices.label: Excise the sheet and apply a replacement graft
answerChoices.rationale: An intact lifted segment over a new fluid pocket does not establish irreversible failure of the entire sheet.

answerChoices.label: Excise the sheet and perform flap coverage
answerChoices.rationale: The previously vascular bed has a localized contact problem, not a newly demonstrated structural need for a flap.

decisionNodes.explanation: A graft can fail because its interface is interrupted despite a viable recipient bed. Correct the new fluid barrier and restore fixation before declaring that all transferred tissue needs replacement.

decisionNodes.stem: Which graft should be favored for {patientName}'s small finger defect after complete scar release?

answerChoices.rationale: The well-supported small functional defect makes retaining dermis useful to limit later contraction; donor closure is feasible.

answerChoices.label: An unmeshed thin split-thickness autologous skin graft
answerChoices.rationale: A thin graft sacrifices dermal support and is more prone to secondary contraction at this recently released crease.

answerChoices.rationale: Expansion is not needed for this small defect and does not address recurrent contraction across the flexion crease.

decisionNodes.explanation: The same graft is not best for every surface. This small vascular defect crosses a functional crease, and retaining more dermis helps resist later contraction. The donor record resolves a real limitation of a full-thickness graft.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The founder reviews the outside hospital's serial free-flap records with {patientName}, who is now well in clinic.
decisionNodes.stem: Which operative assessment should the outside microsurgical team have prioritized at {patientName}'s recorded deterioration?

answerChoices.label: Explore the venous anastomosis and drainage pedicle
answerChoices.rationale: The local congested pattern despite maintained inflow directs urgent exploration toward venous outflow; a persistent arterial signal is not proof of a complete circuit.

answerChoices.label: Explore the arterial anastomosis and inflow pedicle
answerChoices.rationale: The recorded rapid dark bleeding and swelling are more consistent with impaired drainage than isolated loss of inflow.

answerChoices.label: Explore proximal arterial supply to the entire limb
answerChoices.rationale: Stable systemic pressure, preserved flap inflow and a warm opposite limb do not support a generalized inflow failure as the explanation for the local congested flap.

decisionNodes.explanation: The deteriorating flap has a local outflow pattern despite an arterial signal. Urgent microsurgical exploration is required; the observations guide the initial target but do not identify the exact lesion or prescribe its repair.

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Earlier examination
items.value: The flap was soft and pink; arterial and venous monitoring signals were present.

items.label: At deterioration
items.value: The flap became swollen and purple, with rapid refill and dark bleeding on pinprick. The arterial signal persisted; the venous signal changed.

items.label: Other observations
items.value: Systemic pressure was unchanged and the opposite limb remained warm. Loosening external dressings did not reverse the flap findings.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The outside exploration note is now available. {patientName} and the founder review the next salvage decision documented by the microsurgical service.
decisionNodes.stem: Which adjunct is best supported for {patientName}'s residual distal flap congestion after the documented exploration?

answerChoices.label: Monitored medicinal-leech venous offloading
answerChoices.rationale: The operative record has addressed the mechanical pedicle causes; a small persistently congested skin paddle can receive temporary surface offloading under specialist care.

answerChoices.label: Repeat revision of the patent drainage anastomosis
answerChoices.rationale: The current patent anastomosis and diffuse distal venous injury do not provide a new correctable target there.

answerChoices.label: Hyperbaric-oxygen therapy for the congested paddle
answerChoices.rationale: Oxygen delivery does not provide a dependable drainage route; the systematic review does not establish it as a substitute for supported venous offloading here.

decisionNodes.explanation: This is a different salvage phase from initial pedicle exploration. Mechanical causes have been addressed, the distal compartment still retains blood, and another drainage anastomosis has no recorded target. Monitored leech therapy can temporarily offload that selected small compartment.

items.label: Distal venous anatomy
items.value: Exploration found diffuse damaged small veins in the distal skin paddle; the surgeon recorded no additional suitable vessel for drainage anastomosis.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The next outside note records a softer pink paddle during leech treatment. {patientName} became lightheaded when standing, and dressings continued to soak after the leeches detached.
decisionNodes.stem: Which investigation should have been prioritized for {patientName}'s new symptoms during venous offloading?

answerChoices.label: Complete blood count with hemoglobin trend
answerChoices.rationale: Local relief can coexist with continuing blood loss. The new systemic symptoms require assessment for anemia rather than another flap perfusion test.

answerChoices.label: Duplex assessment of the flap pedicle
answerChoices.rationale: The local paddle has improved while ongoing external blood loss accompanies the new systemic symptoms.

answerChoices.label: Prothrombin time and INR measurement
answerChoices.rationale: A normal coagulation result would not quantify the blood loss created by the treatment. Hemoglobin is the more direct initial assessment of this complication.

decisionNodes.explanation: Successful local decompression does not establish systemic safety. Continued bleeding after detachment and new orthostatic symptoms require prompt assessment of blood loss. No hemoglobin threshold, transfusion rule or monitoring interval is specified.

decisionNodes.stem: Which reconstructive procedure should be considered for {patientName}'s persistent elbow extension deficit?

answerChoices.label: Scar release with tissue rearrangement
answerChoices.rationale: The skin band and persistent passive tethering identify a functional cutaneous contracture rather than an elevation problem or isolated muscle weakness.

answerChoices.label: Elbow capsular release with arthrolysis
answerChoices.rationale: The visible skin tether is the supported limiting structure; no intra-articular block has been demonstrated.

answerChoices.label: Tendon lengthening with adhesiolysis
answerChoices.rationale: The band tightens across the skin and limits passive as well as active movement; the record does not localize the deficit to tendon excursion.

decisionNodes.explanation: The scar's boundary classification does not determine its functional importance. Here the skin band remains a mechanical restraint after therapy, so reconstructive scar release addresses the demonstrated target. The exact rearrangement design requires specialist examination.

answerChoices.label: Patch testing to relevant dressing and adhesive allergens
answerChoices.rationale: The delayed eczematous contact pattern calls for an exposure-directed contact-allergy evaluation, not a test of immediate mast-cell activation.

answerChoices.label: Serum specific-IgE testing to immediate latex allergens
answerChoices.rationale: That pathway evaluates immediate latex-protein sensitization rather than the delayed dressing-footprint eruption recorded here.

answerChoices.rationale: Tryptase addresses a systemic mast-cell event, not retrospective identification of a delayed contact allergen. A new exposure should not be created merely to capture a marker.

decisionNodes.explanation: The pattern supports evaluating delayed contact sensitization and selecting relevant patch-test materials. The footprint does not prove which ingredient caused the event; specialist testing and clinical relevance are still required.

decisionNodes.stem: Which interpretation should guide {patientName}'s perioperative allergy evaluation after this event?

answerChoices.label: Retain a perioperative hypersensitivity workup
answerChoices.rationale: The multisystem clinical event remains concerning despite an acute value inside the population interval; the paired record and exposure history still need specialist evaluation.

answerChoices.label: Classify the event as anesthetic vasodilation
answerChoices.rationale: A normal acute marker does not explain away hives and wheezing accompanying hypotension.

answerChoices.label: Classify the event as proven drug-specific IgE allergy
answerChoices.rationale: Even a mast-cell event does not identify the culprit or prove an IgE mechanism from this record.

decisionNodes.explanation: The clinical event still warrants evaluation. A population-normal acute tryptase neither rules out the event nor identifies a drug-specific IgE mechanism. Interpret the actual paired record in its clinical context.

answerChoices.rationale: Changing the skin preparation leaves the confirmed culprit on the device coating.

decisionNodes.stem: Which investigation should be arranged for {patientName}'s recurrent glove-associated skin problem?

answerChoices.label: Rubber-chemical and glove-material patch testing
answerChoices.rationale: A delayed persistent eczema pattern across different rubber products warrants assessment of shared chemical contact allergens, rather than assuming the nitrile label excludes allergy.

answerChoices.label: Repeat serum latex-protein specific-IgE testing
answerChoices.rationale: Repeating the same immediate-protein test does not assess the untested delayed rubber-chemical pathway suggested by this course.

answerChoices.label: Immediate latex-protein skin-prick testing
answerChoices.rationale: This is an immediate protein-sensitization investigation, whereas the persistent eczematous pattern raises a different immune and exposure question.

decisionNodes.explanation: A negative immediate latex-protein assay does not evaluate all glove reactions. The persistent delayed eczema and reactions to more than one rubber product support exposure-directed patch testing for relevant manufacturing chemicals.

answerChoices.label: Isolated resisted tendon examination
answerChoices.rationale: A loose composite fist can remain possible with partial tendon injury. Isolated resisted testing addresses the mechanism and load-related symptom.

answerChoices.rationale: Repeating the already demonstrated low-load movement does not assess the painful load-related deficit.

answerChoices.rationale: Passive motion demonstrates joint movement but does not test the active tendon load transmission at issue.

reviewedSpecs.task: Which coverage plan should the clinic recommend for {patientName}'s currently exposed central tendon?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Earlier treatment
items.value: A dermal template was applied across the dorsal hand defect after debridement.

items.label: Current peripheral surface
items.value: Red granulation tissue with punctate bleeding covers most of the defect.

items.label: Current central surface
items.value: The template lifted from a segment of extensor tendon. This segment is shiny, lacks its paratenon and has no covering granulation layer.

choices.label: Flap coverage of the central defect
choices.rationale: The vascular rim does not supply a graft placed directly on the uncovered tendon. The central surface still needs vascularized coverage.
choices.temptation: Read the central surface separately from the majority of the wound.
choices.counterfactual: A continuous vascular layer covering the tendon could permit skin grafting instead.

choices.label: Split-thickness graft coverage of the central defect
choices.rationale: A thin graft still requires support at its actual recipient surface; peripheral granulation does not establish that support centrally.
choices.temptation: Let the larger healthy area outweigh the small exposed structure.
choices.counterfactual: This is reasonable when a continuous vascular surface covers the central tendon.

choices.label: Full-thickness graft coverage of the central defect
choices.rationale: Additional dermis does not give a graft its own connected circulation and does not solve the uncovered tendon bed.
choices.temptation: Use thicker tissue as a substitute for a missing vascular bed.
choices.counterfactual: A small well-vascularized defect with a need to limit later contraction could favor a full-thickness graft.

reviewedSpecs.explanation: Inspect the entire current bed. Most of this wound has developed granulation, but the segment actually receiving central coverage remains bare tendon. Direct grafting of that segment is unsupported; a flap brings vascularized tissue.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: Covered the key: all three labels name actual coverage procedures; none is a disconnected cartoon flap. The task names the target, not a perfusion rule. Earlier template use cannot select the answer without the current map.

Choose coverage that addresses the uncovered central structure rather than changing graft thickness.

manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Current central paratenon loss and absence of a vascular covering despite peripheral granulation.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: If the central tendon has a continuous viable granulation covering, direct grafting becomes reasonable.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Remove the central row and the competing graft becomes reasonable. Remove the peripheral row and the misleading global impression disappears. Earlier treatment establishes why today's bed must be checked.

items.label: First operation

items.label: Interval course

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Recipient bed at grafting
items.value: Punctate bleeding was documented across the prepared bed.

items.label: New examination
items.value: A localized soft pocket of dark fluid lifts the sheet from the bed. The remaining sheet is adherent. The lifted segment retains an intact epithelial surface.

items.label: Systemic course
items.value: Blood pressure and temperature remain unchanged; surrounding skin is not progressively red or tender.

choices.label: Evacuate the collection and resecure the graft
choices.rationale: The localized fluid barrier is a potentially reversible interruption of contact, rather than proof that the whole reconstruction must be replaced.
choices.temptation: Match the salvage step to the physical barrier.
choices.counterfactual: A fully nonviable graft after bed correction could require excision and regrafting.

choices.label: Excise the sheet and apply a replacement graft
choices.rationale: An intact lifted segment over a new fluid pocket does not establish irreversible failure of the entire sheet.
choices.temptation: Call early discoloration permanent graft death.
choices.counterfactual: Demonstrated necrosis after addressing the recipient bed can justify regrafting.

choices.label: Excise the sheet and perform flap coverage
choices.rationale: The previously vascular bed has a localized contact problem, not a newly demonstrated structural need for a flap.
choices.temptation: Escalate the tissue category instead of correcting apposition.
choices.counterfactual: Persistent exposed avascular tendon or bone after debridement could require vascularized coverage.

reviewedSpecs.explanation: A graft can fail because its interface is interrupted despite a viable recipient bed. Correct the new fluid barrier and restore fixation before declaring that all transferred tissue needs replacement.

manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: If the sheet is necrotic after collection removal, excision and a new graft can become appropriate.

reviewedSpecs.task: Which graft should be favored for {patientName}'s small finger defect after complete scar release?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: After release
items.value: Passive extension is restored. A small skin defect crosses the flexion crease, with a uniformly bleeding subcutaneous surface.

items.label: Neighboring tissue
items.value: Direct approximation recreates the flexed position. Adjacent local skin was involved in the original injury.

items.label: Donor assessment
items.value: A groin skin segment can cover the defect; its donor edges approximate without excessive tension.

choices.label: An unmeshed full-thickness autologous skin graft
choices.rationale: The well-supported small functional defect makes retaining dermis useful to limit later contraction; donor closure is feasible.
choices.temptation: Integrate the functional crease with the recipient and donor findings.
choices.counterfactual: A large defect with limited donor closure or less reliable recipient support can shift toward split-thickness coverage.

choices.label: An unmeshed thin split-thickness autologous skin graft
choices.rationale: A thin graft sacrifices dermal support and is more prone to secondary contraction at this recently released crease.
choices.temptation: Choose the graft that demands less support while neglecting the functional cost.
choices.counterfactual: A broad well-prepared area with limited donor skin and less functional contraction risk can favor a thinner graft.

choices.label: A widely meshed thin split-thickness autologous skin graft
choices.rationale: Expansion is not needed for this small defect and does not address recurrent contraction across the flexion crease.
choices.temptation: Import a large-surface donor-conservation strategy into a small functional reconstruction.
choices.counterfactual: Extensive coverage with scarce donor skin can justify an expanded meshed graft.

reviewedSpecs.explanation: The same graft is not best for every surface. This small vascular defect crosses a functional crease, and retaining more dermis helps resist later contraction. The donor record resolves a real limitation of a full-thickness graft.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: All three are concrete autologous grafts of comparable scope. No option says less contraction; that inference is required. The task does not name a desired graft property.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three autologous graft preparations for the same coverage procedure.
reasoningSteps: Identify that recurrent contraction would reverse the functional gain from release.

items.label: Course

choices.counterfactual: A representative nodule block with relevant deeper tissue could justify additional levels.

choices.counterfactual: A newly changing abnormality at that opposite end would make it a separate biopsy target.

reviewedSpecs.explanation: Scar-like appearance and benign collagen at another site do not establish this nodule's identity. choices.counterfactual: A residual defect unsuitable for direct closure may require a graft as part of a broader specialist plan.

candidate.objective: Identify a correctable loss of graft-bed contact before replacing the reconstruction.
candidate.currentUpdate: The founder reviews two consecutive outside graft checks with {patientName} after discharge.
candidate.task: Which next intervention best fits {patientName}'s graft examination?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Previous check
items.value: The sheet was flat and pink across a punctately bleeding recipient bed.

items.label: Current interface
items.value: A newly raised portion overlies a localized pocket of dark fluid; the remainder remains attached.

items.label: Current tissue examination
items.value: The lifted tissue remains pink and produces punctate blood with gentle dermal abrasion.

choices.label: Evacuate interface fluid and resecure the existing graft
choices.rationale: The new barrier needs correction, while the tissue findings support an attempt to retain the graft rather than excise it. Continued assessment is required; one sign does not guarantee survival.
choices.temptation: Use the interface and tissue observations separately.
choices.counterfactual: A grey nonbleeding detached segment would require a different failure assessment rather than assumed salvage.

choices.label: Evacuate interface fluid and replace the lifted graft segment
choices.rationale: This addresses the barrier but discards tissue for which the record still describes perfusion. The observations do not establish segmental necrosis.
choices.temptation: Correctly recognize the collection but equate lifting with irreversible tissue loss.
choices.counterfactual: Replacement may be needed if examination establishes a nonviable segment after the interface problem is assessed.

choices.label: Increase bolster compression without opening the graft interface
choices.rationale: External fixation does not remove the fluid already separating the sheet from its bed.
choices.temptation: Preserve living tissue but treat established separation as a fixation-prevention problem.
choices.counterfactual: A flat graft without an intervening collection could require a fixation or dressing adjustment instead.

candidate.explanation: Read the interface and the graft separately. A new fluid layer interrupts contact, but detachment alone does not establish necrosis. The described tissue findings support prompt evacuation and restored apposition with reassessment, rather than automatic replacement. No observation guarantees subsequent take.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: The task contains neither collection nor salvage. Two choices evacuate fluid and two retain the existing sheet, so neither a fluid-word match nor the sole-preservation shortcut selects the key. The full fictional examination is visible. The extra negative about grey tissue was removed; actual positive tissue observations carry the viability assessment.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three immediate local graft interventions.
reasoningSteps: Identify a newly developed graft-bed barrier rather than a failure of the originally vascular recipient bed.
Use the current tissue examination to choose attempted local salvage rather than discarding the lifted segment.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Evacuating the collection correctly but replacing a lifted segment merely because it is detached.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: The new interface pocket coexists with pink tissue and punctate dermal bleeding in the lifted portion.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: If the lifted segment were grey and nonbleeding on assessment, the retain-versus-replace judgment would change; if there were no interface fluid, a dressing-only correction could be appropriate.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Deleting tissue findings leaves replacement unresolved; deleting the pocket leaves no reason to open the interface. Intact epithelium alone is no longer used as a viability guarantee.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Standalone clinic chart review. All earlier scored companions are removed. This node supplies the history it needs; no preceding feedback is visible.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate PGY-2/3 author prediction; independent exact-version re-review pending.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: The stated observations distinguish the nearest competing action: The new interface pocket coexists with pink tissue and punctate dermal bleeding in the lifted portion. Counterfactual re-solve: If the lifted segment were grey and nonbleeding on assessment, the retain-versus-replace judgment would change; if there were no interface fluid, a dressing-only correction could be appropriate.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced two whole-sheet destructive foils with local alternative plans, supplied serial chronology and actual tissue findings, and removed the problem label from the task. The supported principle is salvage consideration with reassessment, not a universal viability test. The same repair attempt includes a final label scan: parallel length/category and removal of avoidable key-only noun matching.

candidate.objective: Use recurrent loss of apposition with movement to select a fixation change.
candidate.currentUpdate: The founder reviews {patientName}'s outside graft record after an earlier interface collection was evacuated.
candidate.task: Which next intervention best fits the latest examination of {patientName}'s wrist graft?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Bed and sheet
items.value: The wound bed remains red and punctately bleeding. The sheet contacts it with the wrist at rest.

items.label: Dynamic examination
items.value: Wrist flexion elongates the staple openings and translates the sheet across the bed; the overlying dressing shifts at the same time.

items.label: Fluid localization
items.value: A small fluid layer is recorded between the outer dressing and the sheet. Direct inspection shows contact at the sheet-bed interface at rest.

choices.label: Refix the sheet and add joint immobilization
choices.rationale: The displacement is reproduced by joint movement and loss of fixation. The recorded superficial fluid is not an intervening graft-bed collection.
choices.temptation: Localize the fluid before interpreting the moving interface.
choices.counterfactual: A deep collection lifting a stable sheet at rest would favor drainage; a nonviable bed would require reassessment and debridement.

choices.label: Fenestrate the sheet and drain the deep interface
choices.rationale: The current record places the fluid above the sheet. Opening the deep interface does not correct the reproducible translational movement.
choices.temptation: Repeat the earlier successful drainage without localizing the current fluid.
choices.counterfactual: A collection between graft and bed with persistent separation at rest would make drainage appropriate.

choices.label: Debride the recipient bed and regraft the defect
choices.rationale: The current bed is described as vascular; the new failure is linked to motion rather than demonstrated bed necrosis.
choices.temptation: Attribute repeated separation to failed recipient preparation.
choices.counterfactual: A devitalized bed on reassessment would change the reconstruction plan.

candidate.explanation: The fluid is above the sheet, while the loss of contact is reproduced by wrist movement and failing fixation. Refixation and joint support address that mechanism. Neither repeating deep drainage nor replacing a graft on an otherwise vascular bed corrects the demonstrated motion.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: No motion-related diagnosis appears in the task. The rest and movement observations appear once, and the fluid finding must be anatomically localized rather than dismissed by a blanket no-fluid sentence.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three next interventions for the same graft.
reasoningSteps: Localize the recorded fluid outside the graft-bed interface rather than assume a recurrence of the earlier collection.
Interpret the dynamic staple and sheet displacement and select fixation plus joint support instead of recipient-bed revision.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Repeating deep drainage because a prior collection was successfully evacuated.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Fluid is superficial to the sheet, and wrist movement translates the sheet through elongated fixation openings over a vascular bed.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: A deep pocket holding the sheet away from its bed at rest would favor drainage; a nonviable bed would support debridement and a new reconstruction assessment.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Deleting the fluid compartment permits the drainage competitor; deleting the dynamic comparison leaves fixation versus bed failure uncertain.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Standalone clinic chart review. All earlier scored companions are removed. This node supplies the history it needs; no preceding feedback is visible.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate PGY-2/3 author prediction; independent exact-version re-review pending.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: The stated observations distinguish the nearest competing action: Fluid is superficial to the sheet, and wrist movement translates the sheet through elongated fixation openings over a vascular bed. Counterfactual re-solve: A deep pocket holding the sheet away from its bed at rest would favor drainage; a nonviable bed would support debridement and a new reconstruction assessment.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed the causal task label and the statement that support already corrects the defect. Replaced the thicker-graft foil with recipient-bed revision. Retained necessary bed findings and made the apparent fluid recurrence a different compartment. The same repair attempt includes a final label scan: parallel length/category and removal of avoidable key-only noun matching.

candidate.objective: Select an examination that can detect occult structural injury before labelling a small hand wound uncomplicated.
candidate.currentUpdate: The founder reviews {patientName}'s initial outside hand assessment. Circulation, sensation and wound inspection are being assessed separately; the following functional maneuvers have not yet been performed.
candidate.task: Which functional assessment best addresses the structural risk before choosing {patientName}'s closure pathway?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Mechanism
items.value: A ceramic edge cut the palmar surface of a finger while it was curled tightly around a handle.

items.label: Initial observation
items.value: The small skin opening is now examined with the finger straight. The resting finger cascade looks similar to the other hand.

items.label: Reported function
items.value: The patient can move the finger during light activities but feels focal pain when pulling a loaded handle.

choices.label: Test PIP and DIP flexion separately against resistance
choices.rationale: An injured flexor may still allow gross movement. Testing its separate joint functions against resistance addresses an occult partial injury; neurovascular and wound assessments remain necessary.
choices.temptation: Integrate the palmar mechanism with preserved low-load movement.
choices.counterfactual: A dorsal injury with an extension deficit would direct specific extensor testing instead.

choices.label: Test a composite finger grip against resistance
choices.rationale: A global grip does not isolate each tendon function. Preserved movement or contribution from other structures can obscure the suspected deficit.
choices.temptation: Choose a load test but allow composite movement to mask individual function.
choices.counterfactual: Composite grip may be useful in a broader examination after individual tendon functions are assessed.

choices.label: Test PIP and DIP extension separately against resistance
choices.rationale: This is a real tendon assessment, but it chiefly addresses the extensor apparatus rather than the structures threatened by this palmar injury and load symptom.
choices.temptation: Choose isolated testing but localize the risk to the wrong tendon compartment.
choices.counterfactual: A dorsal laceration with impaired extension would make extensor assessment the relevant target.

candidate.explanation: The palmar mechanism localizes concern to flexor structures. Light movement and an apparently normal resting cascade do not exclude partial injury. Assess PIP and DIP flexion independently against resistance, alongside the complete wound and neurovascular examination; the result does not prescribe a repair technique.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: All three concrete maneuvers are unperformed, so no completed-test checklist reveals the key. Two choices test flexion and two use isolated joint assessment; anatomical localization and isolation both matter.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three specific functional examination maneuvers.
reasoningSteps: Localize the potentially injured functional compartment from the palmar cut and loaded-flexion symptom.
Choose an isolated loaded assessment because preserved light or composite movement can mask partial tendon injury.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Choosing resisted composite grip: it tests load but does not isolate the individual functions at risk.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: A palmar finger injury produces pain under load despite light movement and a near-normal resting posture.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: A dorsal cut with impaired extension would favor isolated extensor assessment; complete painless isolated flexor testing and adequate wound exploration would support a different closure pathway.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Removing the palmar mechanism weakens compartment localization. Removing the discrepancy between light and loaded movement loses the reason not to accept composite function alone.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Standalone clinic chart review. All earlier scored companions are removed. This node supplies the history it needs; no preceding feedback is visible.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate author prediction: near error is a real resisted flexion assessment that lacks isolation. This is not claimed hard or independently passed.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: The stated observations distinguish the nearest competing action: A palmar finger injury produces pain under load despite light movement and a near-normal resting posture. Counterfactual re-solve: A dorsal cut with impaired extension would favor isolated extensor assessment; complete painless isolated flexor testing and adequate wound exploration would support a different closure pathway.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Named PIP and DIP flexion explicitly, replaced passive/composite tests already supplied as completed results, and retained complete examination context. No unverified percentage of tendon damage or repair cutoff is used. The same repair attempt includes a final label scan: parallel length/category and removal of avoidable key-only noun matching.
